entries.a3c9a5249f03cec2a8beda68a28a8a8fceb14dca: <div sID="gen26047" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Luke.15" sID="Luke.15"/> <div eID="gen26047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26048" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26049" type="x-p"/> Evil manners, we say, beget good laws; so, in this chapter, the murmuring of the scribes and Pharisees at the grace of Christ, and the favour he showed to publicans and sinners, gave occasion for a more full discovery of that grace than perhaps otherwise we should have had in these three parables which we have in this chapter, the scope of all of which is the same, to show, not only what God had said and sworn in the Old Testament, that he had no pleasure in the death and ruin of sinners, but that he had great pleasure in their return and repentance, and rejoices in the gracious entertainment he gives them thereupon. Here is, I. The offence which the Pharisees took at Christ for conversing with heathen men and publicans, and preaching his gospel to them, <reference osisRef="Luke.15.1-Luke.15.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. His justifying himself in it, by the design and proper tendency of it, which with many had been the effect of it, and that was, the bringing of them to repent and reform their lives, than which there could not be a more pleasing and acceptable service done to God, which he shows in the parables, 1. Of the lost sheep that was brought home with joy, <reference osisRef="Luke.15.4-Luke.15.7">ver. 4-7</reference>. 2. Of the lost silver that was found with joy, <reference osisRef="Luke.15.8-Luke.15.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. 3. Of the lost son that had been a prodigal, but returned to his father's house, and was received with great joy, though his elder brother, like these scribes and Pharisees, was offended at it, <reference osisRef="Luke.15.11-Luke.15.32">ver. 11-32</reference>.
entries.1aae6b8d6b7e11768d6b2fd494fd4e83af687028: <div eID="gen26049" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26048" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Lost Sheep and Piece of Silver.</title> <div sID="gen26050" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then drew near unto him all the publicans and sinners for to hear him. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them. 3 And he spake this parable unto them, saying, <hi type="super">4</hi> What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it? <hi type="super">5</hi> And when he hath found <hi type="italic">it,</hi> he layeth <hi type="italic">it</hi> on his shoulders, rejoicing. <hi type="super">6</hi> And when he cometh home, he calleth together <hi type="italic">his</hi> friends and neighbours, saying unto them, Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost. <hi type="super">7</hi> I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance. <hi type="super">8</hi> Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find <hi type="italic">it?</hi> <hi type="super">9</hi> And when she hath found <hi type="italic">it,</hi> she calleth <hi type="italic">her</hi> friends and <hi type="italic">her</hi> neighbours together, saying, Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost. <hi type="super">10</hi> Likewise, I say unto you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth. <div eID="gen26050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26051" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The diligent attendance of the publicans and sinners upon Christ's ministry. <hi type="italic">Great multitudes</hi> of Jews <hi type="italic">went with him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.25">ch. xiv. 25</reference>), with such an assurance of admission into the kingdom of God that he found it requisite to say that to them which would shake their vain hopes. Here multitudes of <hi type="italic">publicans</hi> and <hi type="italic">sinners</hi> drew near to him, with a humble modest fear of being <hi type="italic">rejected</hi> by him, and to them he found it requisite to give encouragement, especially because there were some haughty supercilious people that frowned upon them. The <hi type="italic">publicans,</hi> who collected the tribute paid to the <hi type="italic">Romans,</hi> were perhaps some of them <hi type="italic">bad men,</hi> but they were all industriously put into an <hi type="italic">ill name,</hi> because of the prejudices of the Jewish nation against their office. They are sometimes ranked with <hi type="italic">harlots</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.32">Matt. xxi. 32</reference>); here and elsewhere with <hi type="italic">sinners,</hi> such as were openly vicious, that traded with <hi type="italic">harlots,</hi> known rakes. Some think that the <hi type="italic">sinners</hi> here meant were <hi type="italic">heathen,</hi> and that Christ was now on the other side Jordan, or in <hi type="italic">Galilee of the Gentiles.</hi> These <hi type="italic">drew near,</hi> when perhaps the multitude of the Jews that had followed him had (upon his discourse in the close of the foregoing chapter) <hi type="italic">dropped off;</hi> thus afterwards the Gentiles took their turn in hearing the apostles, when the Jews had rejected them. <hi type="italic">They drew near to him,</hi> being afraid of drawing nearer than just to come within <hi type="italic">hearing.</hi> They drew near to him, not, as some did, to solicit for cures, but to hear his excellent doctrine. Note, in all our approaches to Christ we must have this in our eye, to <hi type="italic">hear him;</hi> to hear the instructions he gives us, and his answers to our prayers. <div eID="gen26051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26052" type="x-p"/> II. The offence which the <hi type="italic">scribes</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pharisees</hi> took at this. They <hi type="italic">murmured,</hi> and turned it to the reproach of our Lord Jesus: <hi type="italic">This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.15.2">v. 2</reference>. 1. They were angry that <hi type="italic">publicans</hi> and <hi type="italic">heathens</hi> had the means of grace allowed them, were called to repent, and encouraged to hope for pardon upon repentance; for they looked upon their case as <hi type="italic">desperate,</hi> and thought that none but Jews had the privilege of repenting and being pardoned, though the prophets preached repentance to the nations, and Daniel particularly to Nebuchadnezzar. 2. They thought it a disparagement to Christ, and inconsistent with the dignity of his character, to make himself familiar with such sort of people, to <hi type="italic">admit</hi> them into his company and to <hi type="italic">eat with them.</hi> They could not, for shame, condemn him for <hi type="italic">preaching to them,</hi> though that was the thing they were most enraged at; and therefore they reproached him for <hi type="italic">eating with them,</hi> which was more expressly contrary to the tradition of the elders. Censure will fall, not only upon the most innocent and the most excellent <hi type="italic">persons,</hi> but upon the most innocent and most excellent <hi type="italic">actions,</hi> and we must not think it strange. <div eID="gen26052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26053" type="x-p"/> III. Christ's justifying himself in it, by showing that the worse these people were, to whom he preached, the more glory would redound to God, and the more joy there would be in heaven, if by his preaching they were brought to repentance. It would be a more pleasing sight in heaven to see Gentiles brought to the worship of the true God than to see Jews go on in it, and to see publicans and sinners live an orderly sort of life than to see <hi type="italic">scribes</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pharisees</hi> go on in living such a life. This he here illustrates by two parables, the explication of both of which is the same. <div eID="gen26053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26054" type="x-p"/> 1. The parable of the <hi type="italic">lost sheep.</hi> Something like it we had in <reference osisRef="Matt.18.12">Matt. xviii. 12</reference>. There it was designed to show the care God takes for the preservation of saints, as a reason why we should not offend them; here it is designed to show the pleasure God takes in the conversion of sinners, as a reason why we should rejoice in it. We have here, <div eID="gen26054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26055" type="x-p"/> (1.) The case of a sinner that goes on in sinful ways. He is like a <hi type="italic">lost sheep,</hi> a sheep <hi type="italic">gone astray;</hi> he is <hi type="italic">lost</hi> to God, who has not the honour and service he should have from him; <hi type="italic">lost</hi> to the flock, which has not communion with him; <hi type="italic">lost</hi> to himself: he knows not where he is, wanders endlessly, is continually exposed to the beasts of prey, subject to frights and terrors, from under the shepherd's care, and wanting the green pastures; and he cannot of himself find the way back to the fold. <div eID="gen26055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26056" type="x-p"/> (2.) The care the God of heaven takes of poor wandering sinners. He <hi type="italic">continues</hi> his care of the sheep that did not go astray; they are <hi type="italic">safe in the wilderness.</hi> But there is a particular care to be taken of this lost sheep; and though he has a hundred sheep, a considerable flock, yet he will not <hi type="italic">lose</hi> that <hi type="italic">one,</hi> but he goes after it, and shows abundance of care, [1.] In <hi type="italic">finding it out.</hi> He follows it, enquiring after it, and looking about for it, until he <hi type="italic">finds</hi> it. God follows backsliding sinners with the calls of his word and the strivings of his Spirit, until at length they are wrought upon to think of returning. [2.] In <hi type="italic">bringing it home.</hi> Though he finds it <hi type="italic">weary,</hi> and perhaps <hi type="italic">worried</hi> and worn away with its wanderings, and not able to bear being driven home, yet he does not leave it to perish, and say, It is not wroth carrying home; but <hi type="italic">lays it on his shoulders,</hi> and, with a great deal of tenderness and labour, brings it to the fold. This is very applicable to the great work of our redemption. Mankind were gone astray, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.6">Isa. liii. 6</reference>. The value of the whole race to God was not so much as that of one sheep to him that had a hundred; what loss would it have been to God if they had all been left to perish? There is a world of holy angels that are as the ninety-nine sheep, a noble flock; yet God sends his Son to <hi type="italic">seek and save that which was lost,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.19.10">ch. xix. 10</reference>. Christ is said to <hi type="italic">gather the lambs in his arms,</hi> and carry <hi type="italic">them in his bosom,</hi> denoting his pity and tenderness towards poor sinners; here he is said to bear them <hi type="italic">upon his shoulders,</hi> denoting the power wherewith he supports and bears them up; those can never perish whom he carries upon his shoulders. <div eID="gen26056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26057" type="x-p"/> (3.) The pleasure that God takes in repenting returning sinners. He <hi type="italic">lays it on his shoulders rejoicing</hi> that he has not lost his labour in seeking; and the joy is the greater because he began to be out of hope of finding it; and he <hi type="italic">calls his friends and neighbours,</hi> the shepherds that keep their flocks about him, <hi type="italic">saying, Rejoice with me.</hi> Perhaps among the pastoral songs which the shepherds used to sing there was one for such an occasion as this, of which these words might be the burden, <hi type="italic">Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost;</hi> whereas they never sung, <hi type="italic">Rejoice with me, for I have lost none.</hi> Observe, he calls it <hi type="italic">his sheep,</hi> though a <hi type="italic">stray,</hi> a wandering sheep. He has a right to it (<hi type="italic">all souls are mine</hi>), and he will claim his own, and recover his right; therefore he looks after it himself: <hi type="italic">I have found it;</hi> he did not send a servant, but his own Son, the great and good Shepherd, who will find what he seeks, and will be found of those that seek him not. <div eID="gen26057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26058" type="x-p"/> 2. The parable of the <hi type="italic">lost piece of silver.</hi> (1.) The <hi type="italic">loser</hi> is here supposed to be <hi type="italic">a woman,</hi> who will more passionately grieve for her loss, and rejoice in finding what she had lost, than perhaps a man would do, and therefore it the better serves the purpose of the parable. She has <hi type="italic">ten pieces of silver,</hi> and out of them loses only one. Let this keep up in us high thoughts of the divine goodness, notwithstanding the sinfulness and misery of the world of mankind, that there are nine to one, nay, in the foregoing parable there are ninety-nine to one, of God's creation, that retain their integrity, in whom God <hi type="italic">is</hi> praised, and never <hi type="italic">was</hi> dishonoured. O the numberless beings, for aught we know numberless worlds of beings, that never were lost, nor stepped aside from the laws and ends of their creation! (2.) That which is lost is a piece of silver, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">drachmen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the fourth part of a shekel.</hi> The soul is <hi type="italic">silver,</hi> of intrinsic worth and value; not base metal, as iron or lead, but <hi type="italic">silver,</hi> the mines of which are <hi type="italic">royal mines.</hi> The Hebrew word for <hi type="italic">silver</hi> is taken from the <hi type="italic">desirableness</hi> of it. It is <hi type="italic">silver coin,</hi> for so the <hi type="italic">drachma</hi> was; it is stamped with God's <hi type="italic">image and superscription,</hi> and therefore must be <hi type="italic">rendered to him.</hi> Yet it is comparatively but of small value; it was but seven pence half-penny; intimating that if sinful men be left to perish God would be no loser. This silver was lost <hi type="italic">in the dirt;</hi> a soul plunged in the world, and overwhelmed with the love of it and care about it, is like a piece of money in the dirt; any one would say, It is a thousand pities that it should <hi type="italic">lie there.</hi> (3.) Here is a great deal of care and pains taken in quest of it. The woman <hi type="italic">lights a candle,</hi> to look behind the door, under the table, and in every corner of the house, <hi type="italic">sweeps the house,</hi> and <hi type="italic">seeks diligently till she finds it.</hi> This represents the various means and methods God makes use of to bring lost souls home to himself: he has <hi type="italic">lighted the candle</hi> of the gospel, not to show himself the way to us, but to show us the way to him, to discover us to ourselves; he has <hi type="italic">swept the house</hi> by the convictions of the word; he <hi type="italic">seeks diligently,</hi> his heart is upon it, to bring lost souls to himself. (4.) Here is a great deal of joy for the finding of it: <hi type="italic">Rejoice with me, for I have found the piece which I had lost,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.15.9">v. 9</reference>. Those that rejoice desire that others should rejoice with them; those that are merry would have others merry with them. She was glad that she had found the piece of money, though she should spend it in entertaining those whom she called to <hi type="italic">make merry with her.</hi> The pleasing surprise of finding it put her, for the present, into a kind of transport, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">heureka, heureka</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">I have found, I have found,</hi> is the language of joy. <div eID="gen26058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26059" type="x-p"/> 3. The explication of these two parables is to the same purport (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.7">v. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.15.10">10</reference>): <hi type="italic">There is joy in heaven, joy in the presence of the angels of God, over one sinner that repenteth,</hi> as those publicans and sinners did, some of them at least (and, if but <hi type="italic">one of them</hi> did repent, Christ would reckon it worth his while), more than <hi type="italic">over</hi> a great number of <hi type="italic">just persons, who need no repentance.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen26059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26060" type="x-p"/> (1.) The <hi type="italic">repentance</hi> and <hi type="italic">conversion of sinners</hi> on earth are <hi type="italic">matter of joy</hi> and rejoicing <hi type="italic">in heaven.</hi> It is possible that the greatest sinners may be brought to repentance. While there is life there is hope, and the worst are not to be despaired of; and the worst of sinners, if they repent and turn, shall find mercy. Yet this is not all, [1.] God will <hi type="italic">delight</hi> to show them mercy, will reckon their conversion a return for all the expense he has been at upon them. There is always <hi type="italic">joy in heaven.</hi> God <hi type="italic">rejoiceth in all his works,</hi> but particularly in the works of his grace. He rejoiceth to do good to penitent sinners, with his <hi type="italic">whole heart</hi> and his <hi type="italic">whole soul.</hi> He rejoiceth not only in the conversion of churches and nations, but even over <hi type="italic">one sinner that repenteth,</hi> though but <hi type="italic">one.</hi> [2.] The good angels will be glad that mercy is shown them, so far are they from repining at it, though those of their nature that sinned be left to perish, and no mercy shown to them; though those sinners that repent, that are so mean, and have been so vile, are, upon their repentance, to be taken into communion with them, and shortly to be made like them, and equal to them. The conversion of sinners is the joy of angels, and they gladly become ministering spirits to them for their good, upon their conversion. The redemption of mankind was matter of joy in the presence of the angels; for they sung, <hi type="italic">Glory to God in the highest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.14">ch. ii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen26060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26061" type="x-p"/> (2.) There is more joy over <hi type="italic">one sinner that repenteth,</hi> and turneth to be religious from a course of life that had been notoriously vile and vicious, than there is <hi type="italic">over ninety-nine just persons, who need no repentance.</hi> [1.] More joy for the redemption and salvation of fallen man than for the preservation and confirmation of the angels that stand, and did indeed need no repentance. [2.] More joy for the conversion of the sinners of the Gentiles, and of those publicans that now heard Christ preach, than for all the praises and devotions, and all the <hi type="italic">God I thank thee,</hi> of the Pharisees, and the other self-justifying Jews, who though that they <hi type="italic">needed no repentance,</hi> and that therefore God should abundantly rejoice in them, and <hi type="italic">make his boast</hi> of them, as those that were most <hi type="italic">his honour;</hi> but Christ tells them that it was quite otherwise, that God was more praised <hi type="italic">in,</hi> and pleased <hi type="italic">with,</hi> the penitent broken heart of one of those despised, envied sinners, than all the long prayers which the scribes and Pharisees made, who could not see any thing amiss in themselves. Nay, [3.] More joy for the conversion of one such great sinner, such a Pharisee as Paul had been in his time, than for the regular conversion of one that had always conducted himself decently and well, and comparatively <hi type="italic">needs no repentance,</hi> needs not such a universal change of the life as those great sinners need. Not but that it is best not to go astray; but the grace of God, both in the power and the pity of that grace, is more manifested in the <hi type="italic">reducing</hi> of great sinners than in the <hi type="italic">conducting</hi> of those that never went astray. And many times those that have been great sinners before their conversion prove more eminently and zealously good after, of which Paul is an instance, and therefore in him God was greatly <hi type="italic">glorified,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.1.24">Gal. i. 24</reference>. They to whom much is forgiven will love much. It is spoken after the manner of men. We are moved with a more sensible joy for the recovery of what we had lost than for the continuance of what we had always enjoyed, for health <hi type="italic">out of</hi> sickness than for health <hi type="italic">without</hi> sickness. It is as <hi type="italic">life from the dead.</hi> A constant course of religion may in itself be more valuable, and yet a sudden return from an evil course and way of sin may yield a more surprising pleasure. Now if there is such <hi type="italic">joy in heaven,</hi> for the conversion of sinners, then the Pharisees were very much strangers to a heavenly spirit, who did all they could to hinder it and were grieved at it, and who were exasperated at Christ when he was doing a piece of work that was of all others most grateful to Heaven.
entries.1e783e459284e325b8d7371e62d1b4746f79896a: <div eID="gen26061" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prodigal Son.</title> <div sID="gen26062" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> And he said, A certain man had two sons: 12 And the younger of them said to <hi type="italic">his</hi> father, Father, give me the portion of goods that falleth <hi type="italic">to me.</hi> And he divided unto them <hi type="italic">his</hi> living. <hi type="super">13</hi> And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living. <hi type="super">14</hi> And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he went and joined himself to a citizen of that country; and he sent him into his fields to feed swine. <hi type="super">16</hi> And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him. <hi type="super">17</hi> And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger! <hi type="super">18</hi> I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, <hi type="super">19</hi> And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants. <hi type="super">20</hi> And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the son said unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son. <hi type="super">22</hi> But the father said to his servants, Bring forth the best robe, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on <hi type="italic">his</hi> feet: <hi type="super">23</hi> And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill <hi type="italic">it;</hi> and let us eat, and be merry: <hi type="super">24</hi> For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry. 25 Now his elder son was in the field: and as he came and drew nigh to the house, he heard music and dancing. <hi type="super">26</hi> And he called one of the servants, and asked what these things meant. 27 And he said unto him, Thy brother is come; and thy father hath killed the fatted calf, because he hath received him safe and sound. <hi type="super">28</hi> And he was angry, and would not go in: therefore came his father out, and intreated him. <hi type="super">29</hi> And he answering said to <hi type="italic">his</hi> father, Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment: and yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends: 30 But as soon as this thy son was come, which hath devoured thy living with harlots, thou hast killed for him the fatted calf. 31 And he said unto him, Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine. <hi type="super">32</hi> It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found. <div eID="gen26062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26063" type="x-p"/> We have here the parable of the prodigal son, the scope of which is the same with those before, to show how pleasing to God the conversion of sinners is, of great sinners, and how ready he is to receive and entertain such, upon their repentance; but the circumstances of the parable do much more largely and fully set forth the riches of gospel grace than those did, and it has been, and will be while the world stands, of unspeakable use to poor sinners, both to direct and to encourage them in repenting and returning to God. Now, <div eID="gen26063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26064" type="x-p"/> I. The parable represents God as a <hi type="italic">common Father</hi> to all mankind, to the whole family of Adam. We are all his <hi type="italic">offspring,</hi> have all <hi type="italic">one Father,</hi> and <hi type="italic">one God created us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.2.10">Mal. ii. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">From him</hi> we <hi type="italic">had</hi> our being, <hi type="italic">in him</hi> we still <hi type="italic">have it,</hi> and from him we receive our <hi type="italic">maintenance.</hi> He is <hi type="italic">our Father,</hi> for he has the <hi type="italic">educating</hi> and <hi type="italic">portioning</hi> of us, and will <hi type="italic">put us in</hi> his testament, or <hi type="italic">leave us out,</hi> according as we are, or are not, dutiful children to him. Our Saviour hereby intimates to those proud Pharisees that these publicans and sinners, whom they thus despised, were their brethren, partakers of the same nature, and therefore they ought to be glad of any kindness shown them. God is the God, <hi type="italic">not of the Jews only, but of the Gentiles,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.29">Rom. iii. 29</reference>): the <hi type="italic">same Lord over all, that is rich in mercy to all that call upon him.</hi> <div eID="gen26064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26065" type="x-p"/> II. It represents the children of men as of <hi type="italic">different</hi> characters, though all related to God as their common Father. He had <hi type="italic">two sons,</hi> one of them a solid grave youth, <hi type="italic">reserved</hi> and <hi type="italic">austere,</hi> sober himself, but not at all <hi type="italic">good-humoured</hi> to those about him; such a one would adhere to his education, and not be easily drawn from it; but the other <hi type="italic">volatile</hi> and <hi type="italic">mercurial,</hi> and impatient of restraint, roving, and willing to try his fortune, and, if he fall into ill hands, likely to be a rake, notwithstanding his virtuous education. Now this latter represents the publicans and sinners, whom Christ is endeavouring to bring to repentance, and the Gentiles, to whom the apostles were to be sent forth to <hi type="italic">preach repentance.</hi> The former represents the Jews in general, and particularly the Pharisees, whom he was endeavouring to reconcile to that grace of God which was offered to, and bestowed upon, sinners. <div eID="gen26065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26066" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">younger son</hi> is the prodigal, whose character and case are here designed to represent that of a sinner, that of every one of us in our natural state, but especially of some. Now we are to observe concerning him, <div eID="gen26066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26067" type="x-p"/> 1. His <hi type="italic">riot</hi> and <hi type="italic">ramble</hi> when he was a prodigal, and the extravagances and miseries he fell into. We are told, <div eID="gen26067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26068" type="x-p"/> (1.) What his request to his father was (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">He said to his father,</hi> proudly and pertly enough, "<hi type="italic">Father, give me</hi>"—he might have put a little more in his mouth, and have said, <hi type="italic">Pray give me,</hi> or, <hi type="italic">Sir, if you please, give me,</hi> but he makes an imperious demand—"<hi type="italic">give me the portion of goods that falleth to me;</hi> not so much as you <hi type="italic">think fit</hi> to allot to me, but that which falls to me as <hi type="italic">my due.</hi>" Note, It is bad, and the beginning of worse, when men look upon God's gifts as debts. "<hi type="italic">Give me the portion,</hi> all <hi type="italic">my child's part,</hi> that falls to me;" not, "<hi type="italic">Try me with a little,</hi> and see how I can manage that, and accordingly trust me with more;" but, "<hi type="italic">Give it me all</hi> at present in possession, and I will never expect any thing in <hi type="italic">reversion,</hi> any thing <hi type="italic">hereafter.</hi>" Note, The great folly of sinners, and that which ruins them, is being content to have <hi type="italic">their portion in hand,</hi> now in this lifetime to <hi type="italic">receive their good things.</hi> They look only at the things that are seen, that are temporal, and covet only a present gratification, but have no care for a future felicity, when that is spent and gone. And why did he desire to have his portion in his own hands? Was it that he might apply himself to business, and trade with it, and so make it more? No, he had no thought of that. But, [1.] He was <hi type="italic">weary</hi> of his <hi type="italic">father's government,</hi> of the good order and discipline of his father's family, and was fond of liberty falsely so called, but indeed the greatest slavery, for such a <hi type="italic">liberty to sin</hi> is. See the folly of many young men, who are religiously educated, but are impatient of the confinement of their education, and never think themselves their own masters, their own men, till they have broken all God's bands in sunder, and cast away his cords from them, and, instead of them, bound themselves with the cords of their own lust. Here is the original of the apostasy of sinners from God; they will not be tied up to the rules of <hi type="italic">God's government;</hi> they will themselves <hi type="italic">be as gods,</hi> knowing no other <hi type="italic">good and evil</hi> than what themselves please. [2.] He was willing to get <hi type="italic">from under his father's eye,</hi> for that was always a check upon him, and often gave a check to him. A shyness of God, and a willingness to disbelieve his omniscience, are at the bottom of the wickedness of the wicked. [3.] He was distrustful of his <hi type="italic">father's management.</hi> He would have his <hi type="italic">portion of goods</hi> himself, for he thought that his father would be laying up for hereafter for him, and, in order to that, would limit him in his present expenses, and that he did not like. [4.] He was <hi type="italic">proud of himself,</hi> and had a <hi type="italic">great conceit of his own sufficiency.</hi> He thought that if he had but his portion in his own hands he could manage it better than his father did, and make a better figure with it. There are more young people ruined by <hi type="italic">pride</hi> than by any one lust whatsoever. Our first parents ruined themselves and all theirs by a foolish ambition to be <hi type="italic">independent,</hi> and not to be beholden even to God himself; and this is at the bottom of sinners' persisting in their sin—they will be <hi type="italic">for themselves.</hi> <div eID="gen26068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26069" type="x-p"/> (2.) How kind his father was to him: <hi type="italic">He divided unto them his living.</hi> He computed what he had to dispose of between his sons, and gave the younger son <hi type="italic">his share,</hi> and offered the elder his, which ought to be a <hi type="italic">double portion;</hi> but, it should seem, he desired his father to keep it in his own hands still, and we may see what he got by it (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">All that I have is thine.</hi> He got all by staying for something in reserve. He gave the younger son what he asked, and the son had no reason to complain that he did him any wrong in the dividend; he had as much as he expected, and perhaps more. [1.] Thus he might <hi type="italic">now see his father's kindness,</hi> how willing he was to please him and make him easy, and that he was not such an unkind father as he was willing to represent him when he wanted an excuse to be gone. [2.] Thus he would in a little time be made to see <hi type="italic">his own folly,</hi> and that he was not such a wise manager for himself as he would be thought to be. Note, God is a kind Father to all his children, and gives to them all <hi type="italic">life, and breath, and all things,</hi> even to the evil and unthankful, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dieilen autois ton bion</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">He divided to them life.</hi> God's giving us life is putting us in a capacity to serve and glorify him. <div eID="gen26069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26070" type="x-p"/> (3.) How he managed himself when he had got his portion in his own hands. He set himself to spend it as fast as he could, and, as prodigals generally do, in a little time he made himself a beggar: <hi type="italic">not many days after,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.15.13">v. 13</reference>. Note, if God leave us ever so little to ourselves, it will not be long ere we depart from him. When the bridle of restraining grace is taken off we are soon gone. That which the younger son determined was to <hi type="italic">be gone</hi> presently, and, in order to that, he <hi type="italic">gathered all together.</hi> Sinners, that go astray from God, <hi type="italic">venture their all.</hi> <div eID="gen26070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26071" type="x-p"/> Now the condition of the prodigal in this ramble of his represents to us a <hi type="italic">sinful state,</hi> that <hi type="italic">miserable</hi> state into which man is <hi type="italic">fallen.</hi> <div eID="gen26071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26072" type="x-p"/> [1.] A sinful state is a state of <hi type="italic">departure</hi> and <hi type="italic">distance</hi> from God. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is the <hi type="italic">sinfulness</hi> of sin that it is an apostasy from God. He <hi type="italic">took his journey</hi> from his father's house. Sinners are fled from God; they <hi type="italic">go a whoring from him;</hi> they revolt from their allegiance to him, as a servant that runs from his service, or a wife that treacherously departs from her husband, and they say unto God, <hi type="italic">Depart.</hi> They get as far off him as they can. The world is the <hi type="italic">far country</hi> in which they take up their residence, and are as at home; and in the service and enjoyment of it they spend their all. <hi type="italic">Secondly.</hi> It is the misery of sinners that they are afar off from God, from him who is the Fountain of all good, and are going further and further from him. What is hell itself, but being <hi type="italic">afar off</hi> from God? <div eID="gen26072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26073" type="x-p"/> [2.] A sinful state is a <hi type="italic">spending</hi> state: There he <hi type="italic">wasted his substance with riotous living</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.13">v. 13</reference>), devoured it <hi type="italic">with harlots</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.30">v. 30</reference>), and in a little time <hi type="italic">he had spent all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.15.14">v. 14</reference>. He bought fine clothes, spent a great deal in meat and drink, treated high, associated with those that helped him to make an end of what he had in a little time. As to this world, they that <hi type="italic">live riotously waste</hi> what they have, and will have a great deal to answer for, that they spend that upon their lusts which should be for the necessary substance of themselves and their families. But this is to be applied spiritually. Wilful sinners <hi type="italic">waste</hi> their patrimony; for they misemploy their thoughts and all the powers of their souls, misspend their time and all their opportunities, do not only bury, but embezzle, the talents they are entrusted to trade with for their Master's honour; and the gifts of Providence, which were intended to enable them to serve God and to do good with, are made the food and fuel of their lusts. The soul that is made a drudge, either to the world or to the flesh, <hi type="italic">wastes its substance,</hi> and <hi type="italic">lives riotously. One sinner destroys much good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.18">Eccl. ix. 18</reference>. The good he destroys is valuable, and it is none of his own; they are his <hi type="italic">Lord's goods</hi> that he <hi type="italic">wastes,</hi> which must be accounted for. <div eID="gen26073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26074" type="x-p"/> [3.] A sinful state is a <hi type="italic">wanting</hi> state: <hi type="italic">When he had spent all</hi> upon his harlots, they left him, to seek such another prey; and <hi type="italic">there arose a mighty famine in that land,</hi> every thing was scarce and dear, and he <hi type="italic">began to be in want,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.15.14">v. 14</reference>. Note, Wilful waste brings woeful want. Riotous living in time, perhaps in a little time, brings men to a <hi type="italic">morsel of bread,</hi> especially when <hi type="italic">bad times</hi> hasten on the consequences of <hi type="italic">bad husbandry,</hi> which good husbandry would have <hi type="italic">provided for.</hi> This represents the misery of <hi type="italic">sinners,</hi> who have thrown away <hi type="italic">their own mercies,</hi> the favour of God, their interest in Christ, the strivings of the Spirit, and admonitions of conscience; these they <hi type="italic">gave away</hi> for the pleasure of sense, and the wealth of the world, and then are ready to perish for want of them. Sinners want necessaries for their souls; they have neither food nor raiment for them, nor any provision for hereafter. A sinful state is like a land where <hi type="italic">famine reigns,</hi> a <hi type="italic">mighty famine;</hi> for the <hi type="italic">heaven is as brass</hi> (the dews of God's favour and blessing are withheld, and we must needs want good things if God deny them to us), and the <hi type="italic">earth is as iron</hi> (the sinner's heart, that should bring forth good things, is dry and barren, and has no good in it). Sinners are <hi type="italic">wretchedly</hi> and <hi type="italic">miserably poor,</hi> and, what aggravates it, they brought themselves into that condition, and keep themselves in it by refusing the supplies offered. <div eID="gen26074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26075" type="x-p"/> [4.] A sinful state is <hi type="italic">a vile servile state.</hi> When this young man's riot had brought him to want his want brought him to servitude. <hi type="italic">He went, and joined himself to a citizen of that country,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.15.15">v. 15</reference>. The same wicked life that before was represented by <hi type="italic">riotous living</hi> is here represented by <hi type="italic">servile living;</hi> for sinners are perfect slaves. The devil is the <hi type="italic">citizen of that country;</hi> for he is both in city and country. Sinners <hi type="italic">join themselves</hi> to him, hire themselves into his service, to do <hi type="italic">his work,</hi> to be at <hi type="italic">his beck,</hi> and to depend upon him for maintenance and a portion. They that commit sin are the <hi type="italic">servants of sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.8.34">John viii. 34</reference>. How did this young gentleman debase and disparage himself, when he hired himself into such a service and under such a master as this! He <hi type="italic">sent him into the fields,</hi> not to feed sheep (there had been some credit in that employment; Jacob, and Moses, and David, kept sheep), but to <hi type="italic">feed swine.</hi> The business of the devil's servants is to <hi type="italic">make provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof,</hi> and that is no better than feeding greedy, dirty, noisy swine; and how can rational immortal souls more disgrace themselves? <div eID="gen26075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26076" type="x-p"/> [5.] A sinful state is a state of <hi type="italic">perpetual dissatisfaction.</hi> When the prodigal began to be in want, he thought to help himself by <hi type="italic">going to service;</hi> and he must be content with the provision which not the house, but the field, afforded; but it is poor provision: <hi type="italic">He would fain have filled his belly,</hi> satisfied his hunger, and nourished his body, <hi type="italic">with the husks which the swine did eat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.15.16">v. 16</reference>. A fine pass my young master had brought himself to, to be fellow-commoner with the swine! Note, That which sinners, when they <hi type="italic">depart from God,</hi> promise themselves <hi type="italic">satisfaction in,</hi> will certainly disappoint them; they are <hi type="italic">labouring for that which satisfieth not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa. lv. 2</reference>. That which is the <hi type="italic">stumbling-block of their iniquity</hi> will never <hi type="italic">satisfy their souls, nor fill their bowels,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.19">Ezek. vii. 19</reference>. Husks are food for swine, but not for men. The wealth of the world and the entertainments of sense will serve for bodies; but what are these to <hi type="italic">precious souls?</hi> They neither suit their nature, nor satisfy their desires, nor supply their needs. He that takes up with them <hi type="italic">feeds on wind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">Hos. xii. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">feeds on ashes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.20">Isa. xliv. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen26076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26077" type="x-p"/> [6.] A sinful state is a state which <hi type="italic">cannot expect relief from any creature.</hi> This prodigal, when he could not earn his bread by <hi type="italic">working,</hi> took to <hi type="italic">begging;</hi> but <hi type="italic">no man gave unto him,</hi> because they knew he had brought all this misery upon himself, and because he was rakish, and provoking to every body; such poor are <hi type="italic">least pitied.</hi> This, in the application of the parable, intimates that those who depart from God cannot be helped by any creature. In vain do we cry to the world and the flesh (those gods which we have served); they have that which will <hi type="italic">poison</hi> a soul, but have nothing to give it which will <hi type="italic">feed</hi> and <hi type="italic">nourish</hi> it. If thou refuse God's help, whence shall any creature help thee? <div eID="gen26077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26078" type="x-p"/> [7.] A sinful state is a <hi type="italic">state of death: This my son was dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.15.24">v. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.15.32">32</reference>. A sinner is not only dead in law, as he is under a sentence of death, but dead in state too, dead in trespasses and sins, destitute of spiritual life; no union with Christ, no spiritual senses exercised, no living to God, and therefore <hi type="italic">dead.</hi> The prodigal in the <hi type="italic">far country</hi> was <hi type="italic">dead</hi> to his father and his family, cut off from them, as a member from the body or a branch from the tree, and therefore <hi type="italic">dead,</hi> and it is his own doing. <div eID="gen26078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26079" type="x-p"/> [8.] A sinful state is a <hi type="italic">lost state: This my son was lost</hi>—lost to every thing that was good—lost to all virtue and honour—lost to his father's house; they had no joy of him. Souls that are separated from God are <hi type="italic">lost</hi> souls; lost as a <hi type="italic">traveller</hi> that is out of his way, and, if infinite mercy prevent not, will soon be lost as a ship that is sunk at sea, lost irrecoverably. <div eID="gen26079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26080" type="x-p"/> [9.] A sinful state is a state of <hi type="italic">madness</hi> and <hi type="italic">frenzy.</hi> This is intimated in that expression (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.17">v. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">when he came to himself,</hi> which intimates that he had been <hi type="italic">beside himself.</hi> Surely he was so when he left his father's house, and much more so when he joined himself to the citizen of that country. <hi type="italic">Madness</hi> is said to be <hi type="italic">in the heart</hi> of sinners, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.3">Eccl. ix. 3</reference>. Satan has got possession of the soul; and how raging mad was he that was possessed by Legion! Sinners, like those that are <hi type="italic">mad,</hi> destroy themselves with <hi type="italic">foolish lusts,</hi> and yet at the same time deceive themselves with foolish <hi type="italic">hopes;</hi> and they are, of all diseased persons, most enemies to their own cure. <div eID="gen26080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26081" type="x-p"/> 2. We have here his <hi type="italic">return</hi> from this <hi type="italic">ramble,</hi> his penitent <hi type="italic">return</hi> to his father again. When he was brought to the last extremity, then he bethought himself how much it was his interest to go home. Note, We must not despair of the worst; for while there is life there is hope. The grace of God can soften the hardest heart, and give a happy turn to the strongest stream of corruption. Now observe here, <div eID="gen26081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26082" type="x-p"/> (1.) What was the <hi type="italic">occasion</hi> of his return and repentance. It was his <hi type="italic">affliction;</hi> when he was in <hi type="italic">want,</hi> then he <hi type="italic">came to himself.</hi> Note, Afflictions, when they are sanctified by divine grace, prove happy means of turning sinners from the error of their ways. By them the ear is opened to discipline and the heart disposed to receive instructions; and they are sensible proofs both of the vanity of the world and of the mischievousness of sin. Apply it spiritually. When we find the insufficiency of creatures to make us happy, and have tried all other ways of relief for our poor souls in vain, then it is time to think of returning to God. When we see what miserable comforters, what physicians of no value, all but Christ are, for a soul that groans under the guilt and power of sin, and no <hi type="italic">man gives unto us</hi> what we need, then surely we shall apply ourselves to Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen26082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26083" type="x-p"/> (2.) What was the <hi type="italic">preparative</hi> for it; it was <hi type="italic">consideration.</hi> He said within himself, he reasoned with himself, when he recovered his right mind, <hi type="italic">How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough!</hi> Note, Consideration is the first step towards conversion, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.28">Ezek. xviii. 28</reference>. <hi type="italic">He considers, and turns.</hi> To consider is to retire into ourselves, to reflect upon ourselves, to compare one thing with another, and determine accordingly. Now observe what it was that he considered. <div eID="gen26083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26084" type="x-p"/> [1.] He considered how bad his condition was: <hi type="italic">I perish with hunger.</hi> Not only, "I am <hi type="italic">hungry,</hi>" but, "<hi type="italic">I perish with hunger,</hi> for I see not what way to expect relief." Note, Sinners will not come to the service of Christ till they are brought to see themselves just ready to perish in the service of sin; and the consideration of that should drive us to Christ. <hi type="italic">Master, save us, we perish.</hi> And though we be thus driven to Christ he will not therefore reject us, nor think himself dishonoured by our being forced to him, but rather honoured by his being applied to in a desperate case. <div eID="gen26084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26085" type="x-p"/> [2.] He considered how much better it might be made if he would but return: <hi type="italic">How many hired servants of my father's,</hi> the meanest in his family, the very day-labourers, <hi type="italic">have bread enough, and to spare,</hi> such a good house does he keep! Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> In our <hi type="italic">Father's house</hi> there is bread for all his family. This was taught by the twelve loaves of <hi type="italic">showbread,</hi> that were constantly upon the holy table in the sanctuary, a loaf for every tribe. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> There is <hi type="italic">enough</hi> and to <hi type="italic">spare,</hi> enough for all, enough for each, enough to spare for such as will join themselves to his domestics, enough and <hi type="italic">to spare</hi> for <hi type="italic">charity. Yet there is room;</hi> there are <hi type="italic">crumbs</hi> that fall from his table, which many would be glad of, and thankful for. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Even the <hi type="italic">hired servants</hi> in God's family are well provided for; the meanest that will but hire themselves into his family, to <hi type="italic">do</hi> his work, and <hi type="italic">depend</hi> upon his rewards, shall be well provided for. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The consideration of this should encourage sinners, that have gone astray from God, to think of returning to him. Thus the adulteress reasons with herself, when she is disappointed in her new lovers: <hi type="italic">I will go and return to my first husband, for then was it better with me than now,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.2.7">Hos. ii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen26085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26086" type="x-p"/> (3.) What was the <hi type="italic">purpose</hi> of it. Since it is so, that his condition is so bad, and may be bettered by returning to his father, his consideration issues, at length, in this conclusion: <hi type="italic">I will arise, and go to my father.</hi> Note, Good purposes are good things, but still good performances are all in all. <div eID="gen26086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26087" type="x-p"/> [1.] He determined what to do: <hi type="italic">I will arise and go to my father.</hi> He will not take any longer time to consider of it, but will <hi type="italic">forthwith</hi> arise and go. Though he be in a <hi type="italic">far country,</hi> a great way off from his father's house, yet, far as it is, he will return; every step of backsliding from God must be a step back again in return to him. Though he be <hi type="italic">joined to a citizen of this country,</hi> he makes no difficulty of breaking his bargain with him. We <hi type="italic">are not debtors to the flesh;</hi> we are under no obligation at all to our Egyptian task-masters to give them warning, but are at liberty to quit the service when we will. Observe with what resolution he speaks: "<hi type="italic">I will arise, and go to my father:</hi> I am resolved I will, whatever the issue be, rather than <hi type="italic">stay</hi> here and <hi type="italic">starve.</hi>" <div eID="gen26087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26088" type="x-p"/> [2.] He determined what to say. True repentance is a <hi type="italic">rising,</hi> and <hi type="italic">coming</hi> to God: <hi type="italic">Behold, we come unto thee.</hi> But what words shall we take with us? He here considers what to say. Note, In all our addresses to God, it is good to deliberate with ourselves beforehand what we shall say, that we may <hi type="italic">order our cause before him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">fill our mouth with arguments.</hi> We have <hi type="italic">liberty of speech,</hi> and we ought to consider seriously with ourselves, how we may use that liberty to the utmost, and yet not abuse it. Let us observe what he purposed to say. <div eID="gen26088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26089" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He would confess his fault and folly: <hi type="italic">I have sinned.</hi> Note, Forasmuch as we have all sinned, it behoves us, and well becomes us, to own that we have sinned. The confession of sin is required and insisted upon, as a necessary condition of peace and pardon. If we plead <hi type="italic">not guilty,</hi> we put ourselves upon a trial by the covenant of innocency, which will certainly condemn us. If <hi type="italic">guilty,</hi> with a contrite, penitent, and obedient heart, we refer ourselves to the covenant of grace, which offers forgiveness to those that <hi type="italic">confess their sins.</hi> <div eID="gen26089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26090" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He would aggravate it, and would be so far from extenuating the matter that he would <hi type="italic">lay a load</hi> upon himself for it: I have sinned <hi type="italic">against Heaven,</hi> and <hi type="italic">before thee.</hi> Let those that are <hi type="italic">undutiful</hi> to their <hi type="italic">earthly parents</hi> think of this; they sin <hi type="italic">against heaven, and before God.</hi> Offences against them are offences against God. Let us all think of this, as that which renders our <hi type="italic">sin exceedingly sinful,</hi> and should render us exceedingly sorrowful for it. 1. Sin is committed in contempt of God's authority over us: <hi type="italic">We have sinned against Heaven.</hi> God is here called <hi type="italic">Heaven,</hi> to signify how highly he is exalted above us, and the dominion he has over us, for the <hi type="italic">Heavens do rule.</hi> The malignity of sin aims high; it is <hi type="italic">against Heaven.</hi> The daring sinner is said to have <hi type="italic">set his mouth against the heavens,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.63.9">Ps. lxiii. 9</reference>. He saw that his father had <hi type="italic">taken him in,</hi> and yet he would not <hi type="italic">go in</hi> to him. Note, We think too well of ourselves, if we cannot find in our hearts to <hi type="italic">receive</hi> those whom God <hi type="italic">hath received,</hi> and to admit those into favour, and friendship, and fellowship with us, whom we have reason to think God has a favour for, and who are taken into friendship and fellowship with him. 2. He would not call him <hi type="italic">brother;</hi> but <hi type="italic">this thy son,</hi> which sounds arrogantly, and not without reflection upon his father, as if his indulgence had made him a prodigal: "He is <hi type="italic">thy son,</hi> thy darling." Note, Forgetting the relation we stand in to our brethren, as brethren, and disowning that, are at the bottom of all our neglects of our duty to them and our contradictions to that duty. Let us give our relations, both in the flesh and in the Lord, the titles that belong to them. Let the rich call the poor <hi type="italic">brethren,</hi> and let the innocents call the penitents so. 3. He <hi type="italic">aggravated his brother's faults,</hi> and made the worst of them, endeavouring to incense his father against him: He <hi type="italic">is thy son, who hath devoured thy living with harlots.</hi> It is true, he had spent his own portion foolishly enough (whether <hi type="italic">upon harlots</hi> or no we are not told before, perhaps that was only the language of the elder brother's jealousy and ill will), but that he had devoured <hi type="italic">all his father's living</hi> was false; the father had still a good estate. Now this shows how apt we are, in censuring our brethren, to <hi type="italic">make the worst</hi> of every thing, and to set it out in the blackest colours, which is not doing as we would be done by, nor as our heavenly Father does by us, who is not extreme to mark iniquities. 4. He <hi type="italic">grudged</hi> him the <hi type="italic">kindness</hi> that his father <hi type="italic">showed him: Thou hast killed for him the fatted calf,</hi> as if he were such a son as he should be. Note, It is a wrong thing to <hi type="italic">envy</hi> penitents the grace of God, and to have our eye evil because he is good. As we must not envy those that <hi type="italic">are</hi> the worst of sinners the gifts of common providence (<hi type="italic">Let not thine heart envy sinners</hi>), so we must not envy those that <hi type="italic">have been</hi> the worst of sinners the gifts of covenant love upon their repentance; we must not envy them their pardon, and peace, and comfort, no, nor any extraordinary gift which God bestows upon them, which makes them eminently acceptable or useful. Paul, before his conversion, had been a prodigal, had <hi type="italic">devoured</hi> his heavenly Father's <hi type="italic">living</hi> by the <hi type="italic">havoc</hi> he made of the <hi type="italic">church;</hi> yet when after his conversion he had greater measures of grace given him, and more honour put upon him, than the other apostles, they who were the elder brethren, who had been <hi type="italic">serving Christ</hi> when he was persecuting him, and had not transgressed at any time his commandment, did not envy him his visions and revelations, nor his more extensive usefulness, but <hi type="italic">glorified God in him,</hi> which ought to be an example to us, as the reverse of this elder brother. <div eID="gen26105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26106" type="x-p"/> (2.) Let us now see how <hi type="italic">favourable</hi> and <hi type="italic">friendly</hi> his father was in <hi type="italic">his carriage towards him</hi> when he was thus sour and ill-humoured. This is as surprising as the former. Methinks the mercy and grace of our God in Christ shine almost as brightly in his tender and gentle bearing with <hi type="italic">peevish saints,</hi> represented by the elder brother here, as before in his reception of prodigal sinners upon their repentance, represented by the younger brother. The disciples of Christ themselves had many infirmities, and were men subject to like passions as others, yet Christ bore with them, as a nurse with her children. See <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.7">1 Thess. ii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen26106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26107" type="x-p"/> [1.] When he would not come in, his <hi type="italic">father came out, and entreated him,</hi> accosted him mildly, gave him good words, and desired him to come in. He might justly have said, "If he will not come in, let him stay out, shut the doors against him, and send him to seek a lodging where he can find it. Is not the house my own? and may I not do what I please in it? Is not the fatted calf my own? and may I not do what I please with it?" No, as he to meet the younger son, so now he goes to court the elder, did not send a servant out with a kind message to him, but went himself. Now, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> This is designed to represent to us the goodness of God; how strangely gentle and winning he has been towards those that were strangely froward and provoking. He reasoned with Cain: <hi type="italic">Why art thou wroth?</hi> He <hi type="italic">bore Israel's manners in the wilderness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.18">Acts xiii. 18</reference>. How mildly did God reason with Elijah, when he was upon the fret (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.46">1 Kings xix. 46</reference>), and especially with Jonah, whose case was very parallel with this here, for he was there disquieted at the repentance of Nineveh, and the mercy shown to it, as the elder brother here; and those questions, <hi type="italic">Dost thou well to be angry?</hi> and, <hi type="italic">Should not I spare Nineveh?</hi> are not unlike these expostulations of the father with the elder brother here. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is to teach all superiors to be mild and gentle with their inferiors, even when they are in a fault and passionately justify themselves in it, than which nothing can be more provoking; and yet even in that case let fathers <hi type="italic">not provoke their children to more wrath,</hi> and let <hi type="italic">masters forbear threatening,</hi> and both show all <hi type="italic">meekness.</hi> <div eID="gen26107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26108" type="x-p"/> [2.] His father assured him that the kind entertainment he gave his younger brother was neither any reflection upon him nor should be any prejudice to him (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.31">v. 31</reference>): "Thou shalt fare never the worse for it, nor have ever the less for it. <hi type="italic">Son, thou art ever with me;</hi> the reception of him is no rejection of thee, nor what is laid out on him any sensible diminution of what I design for thee; thou shalt still remain entitled to the <hi type="italic">pars enitia</hi> (so our law calls it), the <hi type="italic">double portion</hi> (so the Jewish law called it); thou shalt be <hi type="italic">hæres ex asse</hi> (so the Roman law called it): <hi type="italic">all that I have is thine,</hi> by an indefeasible title." If he had not <hi type="italic">given him a kid to make merry with his friends,</hi> he had allowed him to eat bread at his table continually; and it is better to be <hi type="italic">happy with our Father</hi> in heaven than <hi type="italic">merry</hi> with any <hi type="italic">friend</hi> we have in this world. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is the unspeakable happiness of all the children of God, who keep close to their Father's house, that they are, and shall be, ever with him. They are so in this world by faith; they shall be so in the other world by fruition; and all that he has is theirs; for, <hi type="italic">if children, then heirs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.17">Rom. viii. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly, Therefore</hi> we ought not to envy others God's grace to them because we shall have never the less for their sharing in it. If we be true believers, all that God is, all that he has, is <hi type="italic">ours;</hi> and, if others come to be true believers, all that he is, and all that he has, is theirs too, and yet we have not the less, as they that walk in the light and warmth of the sun have all the benefit they can have by it, and yet not the less for others having as much; for Christ in his church is like what is said of the soul in the body: it is <hi type="italic">tota in toto</hi>—<hi type="italic">the whole in the whole,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">tota in qualibet parte</hi>—<hi type="italic">the whole in each part.</hi>  <chapter eID="Luke.15"/> <div eID="gen26108" type="x-p"/>

entries.c70152a600d6401474177d74a49afd0b70fcd781: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14573"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 15</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.15.1-Luke.15.32">Lu 15:1-32</reference>. Publicans and Sinners Welcomed by Christ--Three Parables to Explain This.</title> <div sID="gen28176" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14573"/><hi type="bold">1. drew near ... all the publicans and sinners, &c.--</hi>drawn around Him by the extraordinary adaptation of His teaching to their case, who, till He appeared--at least His forerunner--might well say, "No man careth for my soul." <div eID="gen28176" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3edae3aaf5e1506ad4e1446377777ee77392832: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14574"/><div sID="gen28177" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14574"/><hi type="bold">2. murmured, saying, &c.--</hi>took it ill, were scandalized at Him, and insinuated (on the principle that a man is known by the company he keeps) that He must have some secret sympathy with their character. But oh, what a truth of unspeakable preciousness do their lips, as on other occasions, unconsciously utter., Now follow three parables representing the sinner: (1) in his stupidity; (2) as all-unconscious of his lost condition; (3) knowingly and willingly estranged from God [Bengel]. The first two set forth the seeking love of God; the last, His receiving love [Trench]. <div eID="gen28177" type="x-p"/>
entries.b06fa3c6ae7d3951b832f48a3322bdb2e15482af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14575"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.15.3-Luke.15.7">Lu 15:3-7</reference>. I. The Lost Sheep.</title> <div sID="gen28178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14575"/>3-7. Occurring again (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.12-Matt.18.14">Mt 18:12-14</reference>); but there to show how precious one of His sheep is to the Good Shepherd; here, to show that the shepherd, though the sheep stray never so widely, will seek it out, and when he hath found, will rejoice over it. <div eID="gen28178" type="x-p"/>
