entries.2169828e128e9b9bcce952704d9d9b824a61a333:
Verse 30. This thy son. This son of thine. This is an expression of great contempt. He did not call him his brother, but his father's son, to show at once his contempt for his younger brother, and for his father for having received him as he did. Never was there a more striking instance of petty malice, or more unjustifiable disregard of a father's conduct and will.

Thy living. Thy property. This is still designed to irritate the father, and set him against his younger son. It was true that the younger son had been guilty, and foolish, and ungrateful; but he was penitent, and that was of more consequence to the father than all his property; and in the joy that he was penitent and was safe, he forgot his ingratitude and folly. So should the elder son have done.
entries.0b2f51dacf81747685098e62ef0da92ec59f4885:
Verse 31. All I have is thine. The property was divided. What remained was in reality the elder son's. He was heir to it all, and had a right, if he chose, to use it. He had therefore no right to complain.

This instructive and beautiful parable was designed to vindicate the conduct of Jesus--to show that it was right to receive sinners, and that the conduct of the Pharisees was unreasonable. The elder son represents the Pharisees; the younger, the returning sinner, whether Jew or Gentile; and the father, God, who is willing to receive them. The parable had the designed effect. It silenced the adversaries of Jesus and vindicated his own conduct. There is not, perhaps, anywhere to be found a more beautiful and touching narrative than this. Every circumstance is tender and happily chosen; every word has a meaning; every image is beautiful; and the narrative closes just where it is fitted to make the deepest impression. In addition to what has been suggested, we may learn from this parable the following lessons :-

1st. That the disposition of a sinner is selfish. He desires to get all that he can, and is impatient of delay, Lk 15:12.

2nd. Sinners waste their blessings, and reduce themselves to a state of want and wretchedness, Lk 15:13. A life of sin brings on spiritual want and misery. It destroys the faculties, benumbs the mind, hardens the heart, abuses the beneficence of God, and makes us careless of him who gave us all that we have, and indifferent to the consequences of our own conduct.

3rd. Sinners disregard the future woes that will come upon them. The young man cared not for any calamities that might be the result of his conduct. He went on heedlessly--like every sinner-to enjoy himself, and to squander what the toils of his father had procured for him.

4th. Afflictions are often the means of bringing sinners to reflection, Lk 15:14. While his property lasted the prodigal cared little about his father. When that was gone, and he was in the midst of a famine, he thought of his ways. When sinners are in prosperity they think little about God. When he takes away their mercies, and they are called to pass through afflictions, then they think of their ways, and remember that God can give them comfort.

5th. We have here an impressive exhibition of the wants and woes of a sinner.
1st. He had spent all. He had nothing. So the sinner. He has
no righteousness, no comfort.

2nd. He was far from God, away from his father, and in a
land of strangers. The sinner has wandered, and has
no friend. His miseries came upon him because he
was so far away from God.

3rd. His condition was wretched. He was needy, in famine,
and without a friend. So the sinner. His condition is
aptly denoted by that of the prodigal, who would
gladly have partaken of the food of the swine. The sinner
has taken the world for his portion, and it neither supplies
the wants of his soul, nor gives him comfort when he is
far away from his Father's home and from God.



6th. The sinner in this situation often applies to the wrong source for comfort, Lk 15:15. The prodigal should at once have returned to his father, but he rather chose to become a servant of a citizen of that region. The sinner, when sensible of his sins, should return at once to God; but he often continues still to wander. He tries new objects. He seeks new pleasures and new friends, and finds them equally unsatisfactory. He engages in new pursuits, but all in vain. He is still comfortless, and in a strange, a famished land.

7th. The repentance required in the gospel is a return to a right mind, Lk 15:17. Before his conversion the sinner was alienated from God. He was spiritually deranged. He saw not things as they are. Now he looks on the world as vain and unsatisfactory, and comes to himself. He thinks aright of God, of heaven, of eternity, and resolves to seek his happiness there. No man regards things as they are but he who sees the world to be vain, and eternity to be near and awful; and none acts with a sane mind but he who acts on the belief that he must soon die; that there is a God and a Saviour--a heaven and a hell.

8th. When the sinner returns he becomes sensible of the following things:
1st. That he is in danger of perishing, and must soon
die but for relief--" I perish with hunger."

2nd. That God is willing and able to save him--"How
many hired servants have bread enough and to spare."
There is abundance of mercy for all, and all may come.

3rd. He begins to cherish a hope that this may be his.
God is willing, and he feels that all that is needful
is for him to go to him.

4th. He resolves to go to God--"I will arise and go."

5th. He comes to him willing to confess all his sins, and
desirous of concealing none-- "I will say, Father, I
have sinned."
9th. True repentance is a voluntary act. It is not forced. It is the resolution of the sinner to go, and he cheerfully and cordially arises and goes, Lk 15:18.

10th. A real penitent feels that his sins have been committed against GOD, Lk 15:18.

11th. A true penitent also is willing to acknowledge his offences against his parents, brothers, friends, and all men, Lk 15:18.

12th. A real penitent is humble, Lk 15:18. He has no wish to conceal anything, or to be thought more highly of than he ought to be.

13th. God is willing to receive the true penitent, and has made the richest provision for his return and for his comfort. None need to hesitate to go. All who go, feeling that they are poor, and miserable, and blind, and naked, will find God willing to receive them, and none will be sent empty away.

14th. The joy at the return of sinners is great. Angels rejoice over it, and all holy beings are glad.

15th. We should not be envious at any favours that God may be pleased to bestow on others, Lk 15:32. He has given us more than we deserve; and if, by the sovereignty of his grace, he is pleased to endow others with more grace, or to give them greater talents, or to make them more useful, we have no cause to complain. We should rather rejoice that he is pleased to give such mercies to any of our race, and should praise him for the manifestation of his goodness, whether made to us or to other men.

16th. The sensible joy when the sinner returns to God is often greater than that which may be felt after the return, and yet the real cause of rejoicing be no greater. In times of revival, the sensible joy of Christians may be greater than in ordinary seasons. Their graces are quickened, their zeal kindled, and their hopes strengthened.

17th. If God is willing to receive sinners, if all holy beings rejoice, then how should Christians strive for their conversion, and seek for their return!

18th. If God is willing to receive sinners now, then all should at once return. There will be a time when he will not be willing to receive them. The day of mercy will be ended; and from the misery and want of this wretched world, they will go down to the deeper miseries and wants of a world of despair--where hope never comes; from whence the sinner can never return; and where the cheering thought can never enter the mind that in his Father's house there is bread enough and to spare, or where he must feel that if there is, it will be for ever untasted by the wretched prodigal in the land of eternal famine and death.

(x) "Son" Rom 9:4, 11:1

entries.4c82b9abf79dd80dfe210c3836ccfacf238110a6:
Luke 15:10. There will be joy in the presence of the angels. If angels mutually rejoice with each other in heaven, when they see that what had wandered is restored to the fold, we too, who have the same cause in common with them, ought to be partakers of the same joy But. how does he say that the repentance of one ungodly man yields greater joy than the perseverance of many righteous men to angels, whose highest delight is in a continued and uninterrupted course of righteousness? I reply, though it would be more agreeable to the wishes of angels (as it is also more desirable) that men should always remain in perfect integrity, yet as in the deliverance of a sinner, who had been already devoted to destruction, and had been cut off as a rotten member from the body, the mercy of God shines more brightly, he attributes to angels, after the manner of men, a greater joy arising out of an unexpected good.
Over one repenting sinner. The word repentance is specially limited to the conversion of those who, having altogether turned aside from God, rise as it were from death to life; for otherwise the exercise of repentance ought to be uninterrupted throughout our whole life,
“Tant que nous sommes en ce monde;” — “as long as we are in this world.”
and no man is exempted from this necessity, since every one is reminded by his imperfections that he ought to aim at daily progress. But it is one thing, when a man, who has already entered upon the right course, though he stumble, or fall, or even go astray, endeavors to reach the goal; and another thing, when a man leaves a road which was entirely wrong, or only starts in the right course.
“Quand celuy qui estoit du tout esgare tourne bride pour commencer a bien faire;” — “when he who had altogether gone astray turns round to begin to do well.”
Those who have already begun to regulate their life by the standard of the divine law, do not need that kind of repentance which consists in beginning to lead a holy and pious life, though they must groan
“Combien qu’il soit tousiours necessaire de gemir;” — “though it be necessary for them always to groan.”
under the infirmities of the flesh, and labor to correct them.
Luke 15:11-24
Luke 15:11-24
11. And he said,
“Il dit aussi;” — “he said also.”
A certain man had two sons: 12. And the younger of them said to his father, Father, give me the portion of property which falls to me. And he divided between them the property. 13. And not many days afterwards,
“Et peu de iours apres;” — “and a few days after.”
the younger son, having gathered all together, set out on a journey to a distant country, and there wasted his property by living extravagantly. 14. But when he had spent all, a sore famine arose in that country; and he began to be in want. 15. And he went and entered into the service of one of the inhabitants of that country; and he sent him into his field to feed swine. 16. And he was desirous to fill his belly with the husks on which the swine were feeding: and no man gave to him.
“Et (ou, mais) personne ne luy donnoit;” — “and (or, but) nobody gave to him.”
17. And when he came to himself, he said, How many hirelings of my father have abundance of bread,
“Combien y-a-il de mercenaires en la maison de mon pere, qui ont force pain;” — “how may hirelings are there in my father’s house, who have plenty of bread.”
while I perish with hunger! 18. I will arise, and go to my father,
“Ie partiray d’icy, et m’en iray a mon pere;” — “I will depart hence, and will go away to my father.”
and will say to him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, 19. And am no longer worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hirelings. 20. And he arose, and came to his father. And while he was yet afar off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. 21. And the son said to him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, and am no longer worthy to be called thy son. 22. And the father said to his servants, Bring out the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet: 23. And bring the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us feast, and be merry: 24. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.
“Car mon fils que voyci estoit mort, et il est retourne a vie: il estoit perdu, mais il est retrouve;” — “for this is my son who was dead, and he is returned to life; he was lost, but he is found again.”
And they began to be merry.
entries.a634007caeef812b0dd9cca955b67e2f852f735e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.15.11" sID="gen100559" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100560" type="x-p"/>This parable is nothing else than a confirmation of the preceding doctrine. <note n="520"> <div sID="gen100561" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">De la doctrine que nous venons de voir</foreign>;” — “of the doctrine which we have just now seen.”<div eID="gen100561" type="x-p"/> </note> In the first part is shown how readily God is disposed to pardon our sins, and in the second part (which we shall afterwards treat in the proper place) is shown the great malignity and obstinacy of those who murmur at his compassion. In the person of a young prodigal who, after having been reduced to the deepest poverty by luxury and extravagance, returns as a suppliant to his father, <note n="521"> <div sID="gen100562" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Retourne pour demander pardon a son pere</foreign>;” — “returns to ask pardon from his father.”<div eID="gen100562" type="x-p"/> </note> to whom he had been disobedient and rebellious, Christ describes all sinners who, wearied of their folly, apply to the grace of God. To the kind father, <note n="522"> <div sID="gen100563" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Aussi en la personne de ce bon pere il nous propose l’affection de Dieu</foreign>;” — “also in the person of this good father he holds out to us the affection of God.”<div eID="gen100563" type="x-p"/> </note> on the other hand, who not only pardons the crimes of his son, but of his own accord meets him when returning, he compares God, who is not satisfied with pardoning those who pray to him, but even advances to meet them with the compassion of a father. <note n="523"> <div sID="gen100564" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais les previent par sa bonte et misericorde paternelle</foreign>;” — “but anticipates them by his fatherly goodness and compassion.”<div eID="gen100564" type="x-p"/> </note> Let us now examine the parable in detail.<div eID="gen100560" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100559" osisID="Luke.15.11" type="section"/>
entries.0546557a74a9b4ee62fef60af5fbdfaa3e98fff5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.15.12" sID="gen100565" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100566" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.15.12">Luke 15:12</reference>. </hi><hi type="italic">And the younger of them said to his father.</hi> The parable opens by describing a mark of wicked arrogance in the youth, which appears in his being desirous to leave his father, and in thinking that he cannot be right without being permitted to indulge in debauchery, free from his father’s control. There is also ingratitude in leaving the old man, <note n="524"> <div sID="gen100567" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Delaissant le bon vieil hemme de pere</foreign>;” — “leaving the good old man his father.”<div eID="gen100567" type="x-p"/> </note> and not only withholding the performance of the duties which be owed to him, but crippling and diminishing the wealth of his house. <note n="525"> <div sID="gen100568" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais aussi diminue le bien de la maison, et en emporte une bonne partie</foreign>;” — “but also diminishes the wealth of the house, and carries off a good part of it.”<div eID="gen100568" type="x-p"/> </note> This is at length followed by wasteful luxury and wicked extravagance, by which he squanders all that he had. <note n="526"> <div sID="gen100569" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Tout ce qu’il avoit eu du pere</foreign>;” — “all that he had got from his father.”<div eID="gen100569" type="x-p"/> </note> After so many offenses he deserved to find his father implacable. <note n="527"> <div sID="gen100570" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il avoit bien merite de trouver puis apres un pere rigoreux, et qui teint son coeur contre luy iusqu’au bout</foreign>;” — “he had well deserved to find afterwards a father who was severe, and who kept his heart shut against him to the end.”<div eID="gen100570" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen100566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100571" type="x-p"/>Under this image our Lord unquestionably depicts to us the boundless goodness and inestimable forbearance of God, that no crimes, however aggravated, may deter us from the hope of obtaining pardon, There would be some foundation for the analogy, if we were to say that this foolish and insolent youth resembles those persons who, enjoying at the hand of God a great abundance of good things, are moved by a blind and mad ambition to be separated from Him, that they may enjoy perfect freedom; as if it were not more desirable than all the kingdoms of the world to live under the fatherly care and government of God. But as I am afraid that this allusion may be thought overstrained, I shall satisfy myself with the literal meaning; not that I disapprove of the opinion, that under this figure is reproved the madness of those who imagine that it will be advantageous for them to have something of their own, and to be rich apart from the heavenly Father; but that I now confine myself within the limits of a Commentator. <note n="528"> <div sID="gen100572" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pource que ie me tien maintenant dans mes limites, et ne veux point passer l’office d’expositeur</foreign>;” — “because I now keep myself within my limits, and do not wish to go beyond the duty of an expositor.”<div eID="gen100572" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen100571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100573" type="x-p"/>Christ here describes what usually happens with young men, when they are carried away by their natural disposition. Destitute of sound judgment, and maddened by passion, they are ill fitted for governing themselves, and are not restrained by fear or shame. It is therefore impossible but that they shall abandon themselves to every thing to which their sinful inclination prompts them, and rush on in a disgraceful course, till they are involved in shameful poverty. He afterwards describes the punishment which, in the righteous judgment of God, generally overtakes spendthrifts and prodigals. After having wickedly squandered their means, they are left to pine in hunger, and not having known how to use in moderation an abundant supply of the best bread, they are reduced to eat acorns and <hi type="italic">husks</hi>. In short, they become the companions of <hi type="italic">swine</hi>, and are made to feel that they are unworthy to partake of human food; for it is swinish gluttony <note n="529"> <div sID="gen100574" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">C’est une gourmandise plustost convenable a des porceaux qu’a des hommes</foreign>;” — “it is a gluttony more suitable to swine than to men.”<div eID="gen100574" type="x-p"/> </note> to squander wickedly what was given for the support of life. <note n="530"> <div sID="gen100575" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour subvenir aux necessitez de ceste vie</foreign>;” — “to supply the necessities of this life.”<div eID="gen100575" type="x-p"/> </note> As to the ingenious exposition which some have brought forward, that it is the just punishment of wicked scorn, when those who have rejected delicious bread in the house of our heavenly Father are driven by hunger to eat <hi type="italic">husks</hi>, it is a true and useful doctrine; but in the meantime, we must bear in mind the difference that exists between allegories and the natural meaning. <note n="531"> <div sID="gen100576" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais cependant il faut tousiours aviser quelle difference il y a entre les allegories et le vray sens naturel d’un passage</foreign>;” — “but yet we must always consider what difference there is between allegories and the true natural meaning of a passage.”<div eID="gen100576" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen100573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100577" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And was desirous to fill his belly.</hi> This means that, in consequence of hunger, he no longer thought of his former luxuries, but greedily devoured <hi type="italic">husks; </hi>for of that kind of food he could not be in want, when he was giving it to the <hi type="italic">swine</hi> There is a well-known saying of Cyrus who, having for a long time suffered hunger during a flight, and having been slightly refreshed by eating coarse black bread, declared that he had never tasted savory bread till now; so the young man who is here mentioned was compelled by necessity to betake himself with appetite to <hi type="italic">husks</hi> The reason is added, <hi type="italic">because no man gave to him;</hi> for the copulative conjunction <hi type="italic">and </hi>(<foreign xml:lang="el">καὶ</foreign>) must, in my opinion, signify <hi type="italic">because</hi>, <note n="532"> <div sID="gen100578" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Car selon mon avis ce mot et se doit resoudre en Car, ou Pource que</foreign>;” — “for in my opinion this word <hi type="italic">and</hi> must mean <hi type="italic">For</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Because</hi>.<hi type="italic">”</hi><div eID="gen100578" type="x-p"/> </note> and what is here said does not refer to <hi type="italic">husks</hi>, which he had at hand, but I understand the meaning to be, that no man pitied his poverty; for prodigals who throw away the whole of their property are persons whom no man thinks himself bound to relieve, — nay more, as they have been accustomed to squander every thing, men think that nothing ought to be given to them. <note n="533"> <div sID="gen100579" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il semble que ce qu’on leur donne soit autant de perdu</foreign>;” — “what is given to them appears to be as good as thrown away.”<div eID="gen100579" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen100577" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100565" osisID="Luke.15.12" type="section"/>
entries.307efeca4fbb09dae5f63fdcdfd3359b4d6b1d2e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.15.17" sID="gen100580" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100581" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17. </hi><hi type="italic">And when he came to himself.</hi> Here is described to us the way in which God invites men to repentance. If of their own accord they were wise, and became submissive, he would draw them more gently; but as they never stoop to obedience, till they have been subdued by the rod, he chastises them severely. Accordingly, to this young man, whom abundance <note n="534"> <div sID="gen100582" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">L’aise et la trop grande abondance</foreign>;” — “ease and too great abundance.”<div eID="gen100582" type="x-p"/> </note> rendered fierce and rebellious, hunger proved to be the best teacher. Instructed by this example, let us not imagine that God deals cruelly with us, if at any time he visits us with heavy afflictions; for in this manner those who were obstinate and intoxicated with mirth are taught by him to be obedient. In short, all the miseries which we endure are a profitable invitation to repentance. <note n="535"> <div sID="gen100583" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ce sont autant d’avertissemens proufitables, par lequel Dieu nous convie a repentance</foreign>;” — “they are so many profitable warnings, by which God invites us to repentance.”<div eID="gen100583" type="x-p"/> </note> But as we are slow, we scarcely ever regain <hi type="italic">a sound mind</hi>, unless when we are forced by extreme distress; for until we are pressed by difficulties on every hand, and shut up to despair, the flesh always indulges in gaiety, or at least recoils. Hence we infer, that there is no reason to wonder, if the Lord often uses violent and even repeated strokes, in order to subdue our obstinacy, and, as the proverb runs, applies hard wedges to hard knots. It must also be observed, that the hope of bettering his condition, if he returned to his father, gave this young man courage to repent; for no severity of punishment will soften our depravity, or make us displeased with our sins, till we perceive some advantage. As this young man, therefore, is induced by confidence in his father’s kindness to seek reconciliation, so the beginning of our repentance must be an acknowledgment of the mercy of God to excite in us favorable hopes.<div eID="gen100581" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100580" osisID="Luke.15.17" type="section"/>
entries.b853d6939bc762a4e0e95b31cf5a03745d34aa4e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.20" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.15.20" sID="gen100584" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100585" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20. </hi><hi type="italic">And while he was still afar off.</hi> This is the main point of the parable. If men, who are by nature prone to revenge, and too tenacious of their own rights, are moved by fatherly love kindly to forgive their children, and freely to bring them back, when they are sunk in wretchedness, God, whose boundless goodness exceeds all the affection of parents, <note n="536"> <div sID="gen100586" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">L’amour de tous les peres de ce monde</foreign>;” — “the love of all the fathers in the world.”<div eID="gen100586" type="x-p"/> </note> will not treat us more harshly. <note n="537"> <div sID="gen100587" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Sera bien pour le moins aussi debonnaire envers nous</foreign>;” — “will be at least as gentle towards us.”<div eID="gen100587" type="x-p"/> </note> And certainly nothing is here attributed to an earthly father which God does not promise with respect to himself. <hi type="italic">Before they call</hi>, says he, <hi type="italic">I will answer</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.65.24">Isaiah 65:24</reference>.) That passage too of David is well known,<div eID="gen100585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100588" type="x-p"/>I said, I will acknowledge against me my unrighteousness to the Lord and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.32.5">Psalm 32:5</reference>.)<div eID="gen100588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100589" type="x-p"/>As this father, therefore, is not merely pacified by the entreaties of his son, but meets him when he is coming, and before he has heard a word, embraces him, filthy and ugly as he is, so God does not wait for a long prayer, but of his own free will meets the sinner as soon as he proposes to confess his fault.<div eID="gen100589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100590" type="x-p"/>It is wretched sophistry to infer from this, that the grace of God is not exhibited to sinners until they anticipate it by their repentance. “Here,” say they, “is held out to us a father ready to pardon, but it is after that his son has begun to return to him; and therefore God does not look, and does not bestow his grace, on any but those who begin to seek him.” It is, no doubt, true that, in order to his obtaining pardon, the sinner is required to have grief of conscience, and to be dissatisfied with himself; but it is wrong to infer from this, that repentance, which is the gift of God, is yielded by men from their own movement of their heart. And in this respect it would be improper to compare a mortal man to God; for it is not in the power of an earthly father to renew the stubborn heart of his son, as God changes hearts of stone into hearts of flesh. In short, the question here is not whether a man is converted by himself, and returns to him; but only under the figure of a man is commended the fatherly gentleness of God, and his readiness to grant forgiveness.<div eID="gen100590" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.20" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100584" osisID="Luke.15.20" type="section"/>
entries.f896afaf3db7b23b3da0a50db5049235c32f8adf: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.21" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.15.21" sID="gen100591" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100592" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">21. </hi><hi type="italic">Father, I have sinned against heaven.</hi> Here is pointed out another branch of repentance, namely, such a conviction of sin as is accompanied by grief and shame. For he who is not grieved for having sinned, and whose offense is not placed before his eyes, will sooner attempt any thing than think of returning to the path of duty. Displeasure with sin must therefore go before repentance. And there is great emphasis in this expression, that the young man is said to have <hi type="italic">come to </hi>himself, as one whom the wanderings of wild desires had hurried away into forgetfulness of himself. And certainly so far astray are the impulses of the flesh, that any one who gives himself up to them may be said to have <hi type="italic">gone out of himself</hi>, and to have lost his senses. For this reason transgressors are commanded to <hi type="italic">return to the heart</hi>, <note n="538"> <div sID="gen100593" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">A ceste cause en l’Escriture Dieu commande aux transgresseurs de retourner a leur coeur</foreign>;” — “For this reason, in Scripture God commands transgressors to return to their heart.” In the authorized version the passage runs thus: <hi type="italic">Bring it again to mind</hi>,<hi type="italic"> O ye transgressors</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen100593" type="x-p"/> </note> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.46.8">Isaiah 46:8</reference>.) Next follows a confession, <note n="539"> <div sID="gen100594" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Apres la cognoissance du peche s’ensuit aussi la confession</foreign>;” — “after the knowledge of sin there follows also confession.”<div eID="gen100594" type="x-p"/> </note> not such a one as the Pope has contrived, but one by which the son appeases his offended <hi type="italic">father; </hi>for this humility is absolutely necessary in order to obtain forgiveness of sins. This mode of expression, <hi type="italic">I have sinned against heaven, and before thee,</hi> is of the same import as if he had said, that God was offended in the person of an earthly father. And certainly this is the dictate of nature, that every one who rebels against a <hi type="italic">father </hi>rises wickedly also against God, who has placed children in subjection to parents.<div eID="gen100592" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.21" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100591" osisID="Luke.15.21" type="section"/>

“Et l’interroga que c’estoit;” — “and asked him what it was.”

The two adjectives, safe and sound, which occur in the authorized version, are here retained as the translation of “incolumem,” which conveys both ideas; and this is fully justified by our author’s vernacular,” pourtant qu’il l’a recouvre sain et sauf;” — because he hath received him back sound and safe.” — Ed.
28. And he was angry, and would not go in: therefore his father went out, and entreated him. 29. But he answering said to his father, Behold, during so many years I serve thee, and never have I transgressed thy commandment; and thou never gavest me a kid, that I might be merry with my friends: 30. But after that this thy son, who hath devoured thy property with harlots, is come, thou hast killed for him the fatted calf. 31. But he said to him, Son,

entries.f235b4a3de3d5e53a23053f30a6b832b9a533a52: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.15.25" sID="gen100606" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100607" type="x-p"/>This latter portion of the parable charges those persons with cruelty, who would wickedly choose to set limits to the grace of God, as if they envied the salvation of wretched sinners. For we know that this is pointed at the haughtiness of the scribes, <note n="543"> <div sID="gen100608" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">L’orgueil et la presomption des Scribes</foreign>;” — “the pride and presumption of the Scribes.”<div eID="gen100608" type="x-p"/> </note> who did not think that they received the reward due to their merits, if Christ admitted publicans and the common people to the hope of the eternal inheritance. The substance of it therefore is, that, if we are desirous to be reckoned the children of God, we must forgive in a brotherly manner the faults of brethren, which He forgives with fatherly kindness.<div eID="gen100607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100609" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25. </hi><hi type="italic">And his elder son was in the field.</hi> Those who think that, under the figure of <hi type="italic">the first-born son</hi>, the Jewish nation is described, have indeed some argument on their side; but I do not think that they attend sufficiently to the whole of the passage. For the discourse was occasioned by <hi type="italic">the murmuring of the scribes</hi>, who took offense at the kindness of Christ towards wretched persons who had led a wicked life. He therefore compares the scribes, who were swelled with presumption, to good and modest men, who had always lived with decency and sobriety, and had honorably supported their family; nay, even to obedient children, who throughout their whole life had patiently submitted to their father’s control. And though they were utterly unworthy of this commendation, yet Christ, speaking according to their belief, attributes to them, by way of concession, their pretended holiness, as if it had been virtue; as if he had said, Though I were to grant to you what you falsely boast of, that you have always been obedient children to God, still you ought not so haughtily and cruelly to reject your brethren, when they repent of their wicked life.<div eID="gen100609" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100606" osisID="Luke.15.25" type="section"/>
entries.73be2bdce13ec440cf0fcb7b53ab2b702dc309ab: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.15.28" sID="gen100610" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28. </hi><hi type="italic">Therefore his father went out.</hi> By these words he reproaches hypocrites with intolerable pride, which makes it necessary that the Father should entreat them not to envy the compassion manifested to their brethren. Now though God does not entreat, yet by his example he exhorts us to bear with the faults of our brethren. And in order to take away every excuse from wicked severity, he not only introduces hypocrites as speaking, whose false boasting might be confuted, but even affirms that, though any man had discharged, in the most perfect manner, all the duties of piety towards the Father, yet he has no just reason to complain because his brother obtains pardon. It is certain, indeed, that the sincere worshippers of God are always pure and free from this malignant disposition; but the design of Christ is, to show that it would be unjust in any man to murmur on account of his brother having been received into favor, even though he were not inferior in holiness to the angels.<div eID="gen100611" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.15.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100610" osisID="Luke.15.28" type="section"/>

31. Son,
“Mon enfant;” — “my child.”
thou art always with me. This answer consists of two parts. The first is, that the first-born son has no reason to be angry, when he sees his brother kindly received without any loss to himself;
“Veu qu’il n’y perd rien;” — “since he loses nothing by it.”
and the second is, that, without paying any regard to his brother’s safety, he is grieved on account of the rejoicing occasioned by his return. All my property, says he, is thine: that is, “Though thou hast hitherto carried nothing away out of my house, it has been no loss to the for all is reserved for thee undiminished.”
“Ta condition n’en est pas pire; car ie te garde tousiours ton droict entier;” — “thy condition is not the worse for it; for I always preserve thy rights entire.”
Besides, why art thou offended at our joy, in which thou oughtest to have shared? for it was proper that thy brother, who we thought had been lost, should now be congratulated on his safety and return. Those two reasons deserve our attention; for, on the one hand, it is no loss to us,
“Nous n’y perdons rien;” — “we lose nothing by it.”
if God graciously receives into favor those who had been at variance with him on account of their sins; and, on the other hand, it is wicked hardness of heart not to rejoice, when we see our brethren returned from death to life.
“Voyans nos freres estre tirez de la mort, et ramenez au chemin de vie;” — “perceiving our brethren to be drawn from death, and led into the way of life.”

                     </ns0:gap>erving them through his Power by Faith, unto Salvation (for it is upon his Shoulders, that any E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lect Soul is brought home) it is his Eye must find them, and his <ns0:hi>Power</ns0:hi> that must bring them Home) The Country-mans <ns0:hi>Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joycing,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>calling his Neighbours to Rejoyce,</ns0:hi> &c. signifyeth the satisfaction and well pleasedness of Christ, in the Conversi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of Sinners, which is more plainly expressed, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7. <ns0:hi>I say un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to you, that likewise there shall be Ioy in Heaven over one Sinner that Repenteth, more than over Ninety and Nine just Persons, which need no Repentance.</ns0:hi> We have much the same again, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 10. leaving out the Comparative part. There also it is: <ns0:hi>There is Ioy in the presence of the Angels of God.</ns0:hi> We will consider the Expressions in both the Verses together. As to which there may arise these Questions. 1. <ns0:hi>Qu. What is here meant by Ioy in Heaven?</ns0:hi> The Inhabitants of Heaven are God, the bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed Angels, and the <ns0:hi>Glorifyed Saints,</ns0:hi> how can they be said to Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joyce, whereas <ns0:hi>Rejoycing</ns0:hi> is in us the product of a Passion, by which we Triumph in our Union to some good, which we before wan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted. 1. <ns0:hi>An.</ns0:hi> When Terms Expressive of our Passions, are apply<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed to perfect Beings, we must understand them so, as they a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lone can agree to such Beings, separated from those Excesses, which they have in beings more imperfect. <ns0:hi>Ioy</ns0:hi> signifyeth no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing but the full satisfaction of the Will, in a good obtained. Thus God is said to Rejoyce in his People, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 62.5. 2. <ns0:hi>Qu. Who are these Ninety Nine just Persons that need no Repen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tance?</ns0:hi> (For the number, it is but an incertain number put for one certain) 2. <ns0:hi>An.</ns0:hi> Some by <ns0:hi>such as need no Repentance</ns0:hi> under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand, such as think so of themselves, tho indeed they do need it. Others understand it Comparatively, such as if compared with others need no Repentance. 3. Others by <ns0:hi>Repentance</ns0:hi> understand <ns0:hi>Penance.</ns0:hi> Such Sober Persons as stand in no need of a being cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led to a <ns0:hi>Publick Conf<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ssion,</ns0:hi> for the satisfaction of the Church of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fended. I had rather understand it of the <ns0:hi>Glorifyed Saints,</ns0:hi> whose Society Christ left, when he came to Work out our Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />demption. 2. For the others it had been no great matter for Christ to have told them, that God, and the Holy Saints, and Angels, Rejoyce more over one Repenting Sinner, than over Ninety Nine Impenitent Sinners, and self-righteous Persons, who conti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nually grieve him, and whom he abhoreth. But then, 3. <ns0:hi>Qu. How can it be said,</ns0:hi> that <ns0:hi>God,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Angels,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Saints, more Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joyce over one Repenting Sinner, than over Ninety Nine Glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rifyed Saints? An.</ns0:hi> It is universally agreed, that Christ speaks here of God, and of the <ns0:hi>Angels,</ns0:hi> after the manner of Men, Of whose Nature it is to express more Passion, upon a new Object that pleaseth them, than upon others, that they have been long pleased with. As a Parent Rejoyceth more over one Child reco<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vered from the Jaws of Death, than over all the rest of his Children. Tho nothing can be new to God, that is, which he did not see, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ore-know, yet somethings may be new to him in <ns0:hi>facto esse,</ns0:hi> as done and fulfilled, and tho we must not imagine any Muta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, or Alteration of the Divine Being upon any Emergency a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mongst Men. Yet to express how infinitely pleased God is, in the Repentance and Conversion of great Sinners, he is set out, as re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceiving an Augmentation of satisfaction in the effecting of it; such Expressions as these condescended to by God for our Conso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lation, must not be so strained by us, as to occasion any unbe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />coming thought<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of God. <ns0:hi>Qu. Some query how the Angels know of the Conversion of a Sinner,</ns0:hi> and from hence the <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> would some of them infer, that they know our Hearts, because that is the Seat of Conversion. <ns0:hi>An.</ns0:hi> both the <ns0:hi>Angels,</ns0:hi> and the Glorifyed Saints also may know it by Gods revealing it to them.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:314" />8 Either what woman having <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:hi>here <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>sta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted a piece of Silver, is the eighth part of an ounce, which cometh to seven pence half-penny, and is equal to the Roman penny,</ns0:hi> Mat. 18.28.</ns0:note> ten pieces of sil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find <ns0:hi>it?</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 And when she hath found <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> she calleth <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> friends and <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> neighbours together, saying, Rejoyce with me, for I have found the piece which I had lost.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Likewise I say unto you, There is joy in the presence<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> of the angels of God, over one sinner that repenteth.<ns0:note place="bottom">This Parable (as appeareth by the conclusion of it) is of the same import with the other, and needs no further Explication. By both these Parables, our Blessed Lord lets the Pharisees know the end he aimed at in Conversing with <ns0:hi>Publicanes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sinners, viz.</ns0:hi> In order to their Repentance and Conversion, than which nothing could be more grateful, and well pleasing to that God who desireth not the Death of a Sinner, but rather that they should turn from their Wickedness, and live. Of the same import is al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so the following <ns0:hi>Parable,</ns0:hi> which taketh up all the remaining part of this Chapter.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 And he said, a certain man had two sons:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And the younger of them said to <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> father, Father, give me the portion of goods that falleth <ns0:hi>to me.</ns0:hi> And he divided unto them <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> living.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 And not many days after, the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with ri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />otous living.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 And went and joyned himself to a citizen of that country, and he sent him into his fields to feed swine.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to him.<ns0:note place="bottom">The Scope of this excellent Parable, is apparently to Magnify the Grace of God, who is willing to receive and to Treat kindly the greatest Transgressors, seriously Repenting, and turning un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to God; but in it we are also, 1. instructed in the Original State of Man, like that of a Child in his Fathers House, Happy and wan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting nothing. 2. The most Miserable Estate of <ns0:hi>fallen Men,</ns0:hi> such es<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pecially as run to great excess of Riot. 3. The true way of a Sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ners returning to God. 4. The readiness of our Gracious Father to receive, and his wonderful kindness in the receiving and im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bracing repenting, and returning Sinners. 5. The Envy that is sometimes found in good Souls to others receiving (as they think) more favour from God than they do. 6. The Gentleness and Meekness of God in dealing with us, notwithstanding our in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />firmities and mis-becoming passions. God is again here re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />presented under the notion of a Man, who had two Sons. Some that are his Children by Regeneration as well as Creation: he having given them that believe, a <ns0:hi>Right to be called the Sons of God, Iohn</ns0:hi> 1.12. Others, that are his Sons by <ns0:hi>Creation</ns0:hi> only. The latter are here represented under the notion of a <ns0:hi>Younger Son.</ns0:hi> This younger Son is represented, as dissatisfyed with living in his Fathers House, desiring his Portion, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> All Men and Women by Nature were equally the Sons of God, being all in <ns0:hi>Adam</ns0:hi> who was so. All Men Swerved form him, in <ns0:hi>Adam</ns0:hi> all Sinned, all dyed. But some again by Grace are <ns0:hi>returned to their Fathers House.</ns0:hi> Others challenge a Relation to God, as his Creatures, but are not of their Fathers House, but desire only a Portion of the good things of this Life. Some desire <ns0:hi>Honours,</ns0:hi> some <ns0:hi>Riches,</ns0:hi> all of them <ns0:hi>Life</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Health, &c.</ns0:hi> God like a liberal Father, gives some of these good things to one, others to ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther; to some more than one kind of them, whatever they have of this Nature is from him who maketh his Sun to Shine, and his Rain to fall upon the Just and Unjust. Wicked Men when they are thus furnished by God, quickly <ns0:hi>take their Iourney in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to a far Country,</ns0:hi> are more Alienated and Estranged from God by Lewd, and wicked Practices, than they were by Nature. <ns0:hi>Wast their Substance,</ns0:hi> the Health of their Bodies, their time of Life, their Estates, their great and Honourable Capacities, by giving up themselves to Lewd and Riotous kinds of Life, to the high dishonour of Almighty God. It pleaseth God by his Providence, sometimes to bring these Men into Straights; when they are so brought, they will take any base Sordid Course to relieve them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves, rather than they will think of returning to their Heaven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly Father, of themselves they will rather chuse to serve Swine. But if they be such as belong to God's Election of Grace, the Providence of God will no<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> leave them: tho there be little Food for a Soul in the <ns0:hi>Husks</ns0:hi> of sensible Satisfactions; yet they shall not have a Belly full of them. God will bring them off from Satisfaction in any thing, and make every Condition uneasy to them.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:315" />17 And when he came to himself, he said, How ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny hired servants of my fathers have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 I will arise, and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants.<ns0:note place="bottom">Every Sinner is besides himself. His reason Lacqueys to his Lust and Passion, he is Governed by Appetite, and that rageth in him, while his understanding is Blind, and cannot discern betwixt <ns0:hi>Good</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Evil,</ns0:hi> and when he hath in any Measure di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scerned any thing, his Will is <ns0:hi>Stubborn</ns0:hi> and chuseth the Evil. Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />version is but the return of a Soul to it self. The first thoughts of which Conversion arise from a Souls Consideration, what a poor Miserable Creature it is, ready to Perish for ever, whiles never a poor Soul belonging to God, no not the meanest Servant in his Family, wanteth any good thing that is necessary for him. These things increase in a Soul thoughts of returning to his Heavenly Father, through the Operation of the Holy Spirit of God. (For <ns0:hi>of our selves we are not sufficient so much as to think one good thought.</ns0:hi>)</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 And he arose, and came to his father. But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 2.39. Eph. 2.13.17.</ns0:note> when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.<ns0:note place="bottom">The way of a Sinners returning to God must be by arising<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> going to the Father, Confessing his Sins with the Aggravations of them, disclaiming any goodness, any Righteousness in him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self, Humbling himself to God's Footstool, I <ns0:hi>will arise,</ns0:hi> (saith the <ns0:hi>Prodigal) and go to my Father, and say unto him, Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther I have Sinned against Heaven, and before thee, And am no more worthy to be called thy<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Son, make me as one of thy hired Servants. And he arose and came to his Father.</ns0:hi> He <ns0:hi>arose</ns0:hi> from the Sleep, and Bed of Sin, and <ns0:hi>came into his Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther.</ns0:hi> We are not here told by whose Strength, or in whose Assi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stance he arose, and came. We must remember that our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our is here representing a Spiritual Notion, by an ordinary hu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mane Action; now Men have an innate Power to Natural Moti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons, tho not to Spiritual Actions. We are elsewhere told. That <ns0:hi>no Man cometh to the Father,</ns0:hi> but by Christ, nor <ns0:hi>doth any Man come unto the Son, but he whom the Father draweth. E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />very one as he is taught of the Father, cometh unto the Son</ns0:hi>; and again, that tho we be <ns0:hi>saved by Faith,</ns0:hi> yet <ns0:hi>it is not of our selves, it is the Gift of God,</ns0:hi> and Phil. 1.29, <ns0:hi>It is given to us on the behaf of Christ to believe</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> These are but several Expressions signifying by the tender affections, and Gracious reception of Earthly Parents of a returning Prodigal Son, the ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceeding readiness of our Heavenly Father to receive Penitent Sinners; he is so far from discouraging great Sinners from taking up thoughts of returning unto him, that he cherisheth the <ns0:hi>Em<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bryoes</ns0:hi> of such Resolutions, <ns0:hi>I said</ns0:hi> (saith the <ns0:hi>Psalmist) I will confess my Transgressions unto the Lord, and thou forg avest the Iniquity of my Sin, Psal.</ns0:hi> 32.5. God seeth the first good Motions, and stirrings of our Hearts, towards him, and he needs must do so<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> for he stirreth them up in us; there is no sacred Fire upon our Altar, but first cometh down from Heaven, whiles yet the Soul is far off from believing, and closing with Christ actually, and hath but some thoughts of that tendency, God looks upon it, incourageth it, meeteth it as it were half-way; and indeed if he did not, our Goodness would be but like a Morn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Dew, which would quickly pass away, our first Inclinations would perish like an untimely Birth, before it hath seen the Light.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 And the son said unto him, Father, I have sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned against heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son.<ns0:note place="bottom">Now the good thoughts, and Resolutions of the Sinner ri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pen into Action, and the first of it is an Expression of his Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />victions, and Humiliation by an humble Confession of his Sins, with their Aggravations, as committed against God, and that in the sight of God, and this <ns0:hi>God, his Father,</ns0:hi> his unworthiness so much as of the Name of a Son to such a Father. The Petiti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />onary part of what he resolved upon, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19. is not here again re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />peated, but to be understood. Men may by the common Grace of God denyed to no Man, have some good thoughts, but they dye away, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>d <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> to no Maturity, unless the Holy Spirit of God breath<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> upon them, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, and upholdeth them in the Soul, but where the Lord designeth a thorough Change in a Soul, the Spirit of the Lord comes, and convinceth the Soul of Sin, and of <ns0:hi>Righteousness,</ns0:hi> and where he doth so<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> the Resolution ri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />peneth into Action, and produceth in the Soul a true and hear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty Contrition, and confession of its sin, with humble Petitions and a Resignation of its self to the Lords Will, and a casting of its self upon God's free Grace and Mercy.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 But the father said to his servants, Bring forth the best robe, and put <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> feet.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi>; and let us eat and be merry.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry.<ns0:note place="bottom">We must remember that we are in a <ns0:hi>Parable</ns0:hi> where a Sinner is represented to us, under the notion of a Prodigal Son, God un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der the notion of an Indulgent Father. A <ns0:hi>Repenting Sinner,</ns0:hi> under the notion of a Prodigal returning to his Father, Confes<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing his Error, Petitioning his Father for Mercy, acknowledging he deserveth none, but casting himself upon his Fathers Good<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness and Mercy. It is observed by an Eminent Author, That amongst all the <ns0:hi>Parables,</ns0:hi> this is one of the most famous, and wherein is the most full and perfect Representation of the thing intended to be represented, and an Applicableness of every part of the Similitude to that which it is brought to represent. This part of it representeth the Grace of God to truly repenting Sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ners. We before heard, his readiness, and willingness to receive them, this part lets us see the manner how he will treat them. As in case of Apostacy; the seeming Righteousness, and Profession of Men shall not be remembred, <ns0:hi>Ezech.</ns0:hi> 3.20. and 33.13. so in case of a true and hearty Repentance, the Sins of a Soul shall not be remembred, <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> 43.25. The <ns0:hi>Father</ns0:hi> taketh no notice of the Prodigal's leaving his Father's House, or wasting his Estate Rio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tously, but saith, <ns0:hi>Bring forth the best Robe</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, and <ns0:hi>put a Ring upon his Hand, and Shoes upon his Feet,</ns0:hi> and bring hither <ns0:hi>the Fatted Calf</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. I find some Interpreters, who by the Fatted Calf are willing enough to understand Christ; yet Interpreting the <ns0:hi>best Robe, Innocen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Inherent Righteousness.</ns0:hi> Nor is it an ill Interpretation, if we consider, That God at the same time, when he imputeth the Merits of Christ to the Soul for <ns0:hi>Iustification,</ns0:hi> doth also put his <ns0:hi>Spirit of Holiness</ns0:hi> into the Soul, by which being renewed in the inward Man, this Man brings forth the Fruits of <ns0:hi>Holiness unto Righteousness, Ezech.</ns0:hi> 36.26, 27. But why we should not understand both the Phrases of the Application of Christ's Merits, and the Imputation of his Righteousness to the Soul, I cannot tell, considering, that the Church of <ns0:hi>Laodicea</ns0:hi> is Counsel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led to buy of him <ns0:hi>White Rayment, that she might be Cloathed Rev.</ns0:hi> 3.18. and that those <ns0:hi>Cloathed with White Robes, Rev.</ns0:hi> 7.14. are said to have <ns0:hi>Washed their Robes,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>made them White in the Blood of the Lamb,</ns0:hi> and that tho the Habits of Grace are sometimes in Holy Writ, compared to <ns0:hi>Cloathing. Be ye Cloath<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed with Humility</ns0:hi> (saith the Apostle) yet these are not <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, I should therefore rather chuse, to Interpret the <ns0:hi>killing of the Fatted Calf for the Prodigal Son,</ns0:hi> as representing, that Application of the Blood of Christ, which is made to every Sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner, that truly repenteth, and maketh its application to God for Mercy; and the <ns0:hi>best Robe,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Righteousness of Christ,</ns0:hi> in that moment reckoned unto the Soul (thus believing) for Righteousness; further yet (to consider it only in the Parable) the Word <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Sacrifice the Fatted Calf, seems to signify what a great cause of thanksgiving to God, as well as <ns0:hi>joy amongst Men,</ns0:hi> the Conversion of a Sinner is. We that are earthly Parents, or Ministers of the Gospel, should not receive the news, or set the visible probability of a Souls being converted, and returning unto God, without offering a Sacrifice of thanksgiving unto God, for doing such things for Men, and without a true, and hearty re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joycing in our selves. But to return again to the meaning of the Parable, <ns0:hi>let us eat and be Merry,</ns0:hi> consider these Words, as the Words of an <ns0:hi>Heavenly Father,</ns0:hi> they signifie unto us, that the eternal God, from the Day that a repenting Soul, hath the Blood of Christ applyed to it, and is cloathed with his righteousness, is at Peace with the Soul, hath a Communion with it, and that it from that time, hath a true right to spiritual Mirth, and rejoycing, <ns0:hi>for Light is sown for the Righteous, and joy for the upright in heart</ns0:hi>; tho possibly the Soul at present through temptations, cannot ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prehend it, and be not actually possessed of that <ns0:hi>joy, and Peace which followeth believing,</ns0:hi> yet it hath a right to it, and indeed none but that Soul hath any thing to do with Peace. It followeth, <ns0:hi>For this my Son was dead, and is alive again, he was lost and is found.</ns0:hi> A Sinful Soul is a dead Soul, as the Woman that li<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veth in Pleasure, is said to be <ns0:hi>Dead while she lives,</ns0:hi> by the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle. The Conversion of a Sinner, is as a Resurrection from the Dead. Nor is any Soul capable of any true Mirth, till it be Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />conciled to God through the Blood of Christ.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 Now his elder son was in the field: and as he came and drew nigh to the house, he heard mu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sick and dancing.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 And he called one of the servants, and asked what these things meant.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 And he said unto him, Thy Brother is come<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and thy father hath killed the fatted calf, because he hath received him safe and sound.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 And he was angry and would not go in: there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore came his father out, and intreated him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 And he answering, said to <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> father, Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment, and yet thou never ga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:315" />30 But as soon as this thy son was come, which hath devoured thy living with harlots, thou hast kil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led for him the fatted calf.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 And he said unto him, Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found.<ns0:note place="bottom">This last part of the <ns0:hi>Parable,</ns0:hi> is not so exactly applicable to that which it is brought to represent, as the former parts are. But it serveth excellently to shew us that <ns0:hi>Envy,</ns0:hi> which is found in our Hearts by Nature, to the <ns0:hi>Spiritual Good,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>advantage</ns0:hi> of others. Two things are observable in it. <ns0:hi>1. Mans Peevishness</ns0:hi> and Envy. 2. <ns0:hi>Gods Meekness</ns0:hi> towards us under our <ns0:hi>Frowardness</ns0:hi> By the eldest Son some think, the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> are represented, whose Peevishness to the <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> and the offer of the Grace of the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel to them, is made appear to us from many places of Holy Writ. Others think that by the <ns0:hi>Eldest Son</ns0:hi> are represented <ns0:hi>Hy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pocrites,</ns0:hi> who swelling in an opinion of themselves, and their own Righteousness have no Patience to hear, that any others should be preferred in the favour of God before them. Why may not we say that <ns0:hi>All</ns0:hi> are understood by it, even the best of Gods People, who (if they narrowly search their own Hearts) will find something of <ns0:hi>Pride</ns0:hi> and Envy remaining in the best of them, and as the former prompts them to judge themselves as much deserving the <ns0:hi>Favour of God,</ns0:hi> even in special particular Dispensations as any others: So the latter inclineth them to re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pine at such Dispensations of Divine Grace, as others receive, and they want. Two Corruptions which we are as much concerned to keep a Watch upon, or against, as any other, speaking both a Peevishness to the Honour and Glory of God, a Dissatisfaction in his Dispensations, and an Offer at the Controulment of his Wisdom and Justice, and also a great Degree of uncharitableness; our Eye being Evil because the Lord is Good, besides, that it seemeth to put in a claim of Merit; and the Soul that Indulgeth it self in such thoughts, seems to say that he hath deserved more, than it doth receive; for without such a supposition, it is the most unreasonable thing imaginable, that any Person should be displeased, that another should have a greater share in the Favour of God than he, whiles himself receives more than he can lay a claim unto, and God may do with his own what he pleaseth. The Meekness of God in dealing with us under our Frowardness, is as much remarkable. <ns0:hi>Son</ns0:hi> (saith this Father in the <ns0:hi>Parable) thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine. It was Meet that we should make Merry, and be glad, for this thy Brother was Dead, and is alive again, was lost, and is found.</ns0:hi> This must be understood of God <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> as spoken af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter the manner of Men, who shew greater passions upon the re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceiving of <ns0:hi>a Good</ns0:hi> that is new to them, and possibly surprizing, than they ordinarily shew upon the view of a good of which they have had longer Fruition, so it confirms what was before said in <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7.10. we must take heed of thinking that anything can make a change or alteration in God, but must look upon it only as an expres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion of Gods high satisfaction, and well pleasedness in a Sinne<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Conversion, and turning unto him, so as if it were possible any good should more than other affect the Divine Being, it would be this, so as this whole Parable is of excellent use, not only to in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />struct Sinners in their miserable State, till they be reconciled to God, but to deliver them from all Temptations to Fear, that heartily returning they shall not be accepted.</ns0:note>
